name: Cabernet Sauvignon
description:
**Cabernet Sauvignon** is a red grape born in Bordeaux from a natural crossing of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc, and it has become the most planted premium red variety on the planet, the backbone of countless age-worthy wines.

**In the glass** — expect a deep, almost opaque ruby colour, aromas of blackcurrant, cassis, cedar and graphite, and a firm, structured palate driven by high tannin, bright acidity and full body.

**Where it grows** — it is the anchor of the Médoc in Bordeaux, thrives in Napa Valley and Coonawarra, and produces bold, ripe styles in Chile, Argentina and South Africa; cooler sites lean herbal and savoury while warmer ones give riper, plusher fruit.

**At the table** — a natural match for a grilled ribeye or roast lamb.

**Cellaring** — its tannin and acidity make it a superb ager, and top examples reward a decade or more in the bottle.

name: Pinot Noir
description:
**Pinot Noir** is a red grape from Burgundy, one of the oldest and most revered varieties in the world, famous for being thin-skinned, fussy to grow and capable of extraordinary elegance. It is also known as Pinot Nero in Italy.

**In the glass** — pale to medium ruby, with perfumed aromas of red cherry, raspberry, rose and, with age, forest floor and mushroom; the palate is light to medium bodied with silky tannin and vibrant acidity.

**Where it grows** — Burgundy is the benchmark, but it excels in Oregon, California's Sonoma Coast, New Zealand's Central Otago and Germany, where cool climates preserve its delicacy; warmer sites give riper, fruitier wines.

**At the table** — lovely with roast duck, salmon or mushroom dishes.

**Cellaring** — the best bottlings age gracefully for a decade or more, though many are delicious young.

name: Chardonnay
description:
**Chardonnay** is a white grape from Burgundy that has spread to nearly every wine-growing region on earth, prized for its versatility and its ability to reflect both terroir and the winemaker's hand.

**In the glass** — colour ranges from pale straw to golden; unoaked versions show green apple, citrus and pear with crisp acidity, while oak-aged and malolactic styles add butter, hazelnut and a rounder, fuller body.

**Where it grows** — Burgundy's Chablis and Côte de Beaune set the standard, but it shines in California, Australia, New Zealand and Italy; cool climates give lean, mineral wines while warm regions produce ripe, tropical ones. It is also a key grape in Champagne.

**At the table** — pairs beautifully with roast chicken, lobster or creamy pasta.

**Cellaring** — crisp styles are best young, but fine oaked and Burgundian examples can age for many years.

name: Syrah
description:
**Syrah** is a red grape from the Northern Rhône in France, responsible for some of the world's most dramatic, savoury reds. Under the name Shiraz it became the flagship variety of Australia.

**In the glass** — deep purple-black in colour, with aromas of blackberry, black pepper, smoked meat and violet; the palate is full bodied with firm tannin and moderate acidity.

**Where it grows** — the Northern Rhône appellations of Hermitage and Côte-Rôtie are its spiritual home, giving peppery, elegant wines, while Australia's Barossa Valley produces richer, jammier Shiraz; it also does well in the Southern Rhône blends, South Africa, Chile and Washington State.

**At the table** — excellent with grilled meats, game and hearty stews.

**Cellaring** — structured Northern Rhône and top Australian examples age superbly for a decade or more.

name: Merlot
description:
**Merlot** is a red grape from Bordeaux, one of the world's most planted varieties, valued for its softness, generosity and its role as a blending partner to Cabernet Sauvignon.

**In the glass** — medium to deep ruby, with aromas of plum, black cherry, chocolate and herbs; the palate is plush and round, with softer tannin, medium acidity and a supple, medium to full body.

**Where it grows** — it dominates Bordeaux's Right Bank in Pomerol and Saint-Émilion, where it can reach remarkable heights, and is widely grown in California, Italy, Chile and Washington State; cooler sites lean toward structure and savoury notes while warmer ones give riper, fleshier fruit.

**At the table** — versatile with roast pork, poultry and mushroom dishes.

**Cellaring** — approachable young, yet the finest Right Bank bottlings age beautifully for many years.

name: Cabernet Franc
description:
**Cabernet Franc** is a red grape grown in both Bordeaux and the Loire Valley, and is one of the parent grapes of Cabernet Sauvignon. It ripens earlier than its offspring and brings perfume and freshness to blends.

**In the glass** — medium ruby in colour, with aromas of raspberry, bell pepper, graphite and violet; the palate is medium bodied with lively acidity and moderate, fine-grained tannin.

**Where it grows** — in Bordeaux it is a supporting player alongside Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon, while in the Loire's Chinon and Bourgueil it makes vibrant, savoury varietal reds; it also succeeds in Italy, California and Argentina, showing riper fruit in warmer climates.

**At the table** — pairs well with roast vegetables, charcuterie and grilled meats.

**Cellaring** — enjoyable young, though structured examples reward several years of ageing.

name: Riesling
description:
**Riesling** is a white grape from Germany's Rhine region, widely regarded as one of the noblest white varieties for its purity, transparency and ability to express place with startling precision.

**In the glass** — pale in colour, with aromas of lime, green apple, apricot and, with age, a distinctive petrol note; the palate is bracingly high in acidity, light bodied and can range from bone dry to lusciously sweet.

**Where it grows** — Germany's Mosel and Rheingau are the benchmarks, giving delicate, mineral wines, while Alsace produces richer dry styles and Austria, Australia's Clare and Eden Valleys and Washington State add their own signatures.

**At the table** — superb with spicy Asian dishes, pork and shellfish.

**Cellaring** — one of the great agers among whites, evolving remarkably over one to several decades.

name: Grenache
description:
**Grenache** is a red grape that originated in the Aragón region of Spain, where it is called Garnacha, and it is widely grown across the Mediterranean. It is also known as Cannonau in Sardinia and Garnacho.

**In the glass** — typically pale to medium ruby, with aromas of ripe strawberry, red plum, white pepper and dried herbs; the palate is generous and warming, with high alcohol, soft tannin and medium acidity.

**Where it grows** — it is the backbone of Southern Rhône blends such as Châteauneuf-du-Pape, thrives across Spain in Priorat and Rioja, and produces old-vine wines in Australia's Barossa and in Sardinia.

**At the table** — a fine partner for grilled lamb, stews and roasted vegetables.

**Cellaring** — often delicious young, but old-vine and blended examples can age well for many years.

name: Sangiovese
description:
**Sangiovese** is a red grape and the signature variety of Tuscany, the heart of Italy's most famous reds. On the island of Corsica it is known as Nielluccio.

**In the glass** — medium ruby, sometimes with a garnet tinge, offering aromas of sour cherry, red plum, tomato leaf and dried herbs; the palate is savoury, with high acidity, firm and grippy tannin and medium body.

**Where it grows** — it is the sole or dominant grape of Chianti, Brunello di Montalcino and Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, each expressing a different weight and structure, and it also features in Super Tuscan blends; beyond Italy it appears in California, Argentina and Australia.

**At the table** — made for tomato-based pasta, pizza and grilled meats.

**Cellaring** — top Brunello and Chianti Classico examples age gracefully for a decade or more.

name: Pinot Meunier
description:
**Pinot Meunier** is a red grape from the Champagne region of France, where it is one of the three principal varieties used in Champagne alongside Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. It is also known simply as Meunier, and as Schwarzriesling in Germany.

**In the glass** — as a still red it is medium ruby with aromas of red berries and earth; in sparkling blends it contributes fruitiness, roundness and approachability, with moderate acidity and a soft, supple character.

**Where it grows** — its stronghold is Champagne, particularly the cooler Marne Valley, where it buds late and ripens early, making it reliable in a marginal climate; small plantings also exist in Germany and increasingly for varietal sparkling wines elsewhere.

**At the table** — lovely with soft cheeses, poultry and canapés.

**Cellaring** — it lends early charm to blends, and while most is enjoyed young, some varietal wines can develop with time.

name: Petit Verdot
description:
**Petit Verdot** is a red grape from Bordeaux, traditionally a minor blending component that adds colour, tannin and aromatic lift to Cabernet-based wines. Its name reflects its small, late-ripening berries.

**In the glass** — deeply coloured, almost inky, with aromas of blackberry, violet, dried herbs and spice; the palate is full bodied with firm tannin, good acidity and a dense, structured feel.

**Where it grows** — in Bordeaux it plays a supporting role in the Médoc, where it ripens reliably only in warm vintages, but in sunnier climates such as California, Spain, Australia and Argentina it increasingly stands alone as a bold varietal wine.

**At the table** — pairs well with braised beef, venison and rich, spiced dishes.

**Cellaring** — its tannin and structure make it well suited to ageing for several years or more.

name: Tempranillo
description:
**Tempranillo** is a red grape and the backbone of Spanish fine wine, most famously in Rioja and Ribera del Duero, where it produces the country's most age-worthy reds. Its name nods to its habit of ripening early.

**In the glass** — expect a medium-to-full red with aromas of red cherry, dried fig, leather and, when oak-aged, sweet vanilla and dill from American barrels. Tannins are firm but rounded, acidity moderate, and the wine gains a savoury, tobacco-like character with age.

**Where it grows** — Rioja gives elegant, oak-scented wines; Ribera del Duero produces darker, more powerful ones. In Portugal it turns up as Tinta Roriz and Aragonez, a key player in Port and Douro reds, and it has spread to Australia, Argentina and beyond.

**At the table** — a natural partner for roast lamb, chorizo and other grilled or cured meats.

**Cellaring** — the best Gran Reserva bottlings reward a decade or two, though everyday styles drink beautifully within a few years.

name: Mourvèdre
description:
**Mourvèdre** is a red grape of Spanish origin, at home around Valencia and Murcia, where it is called Monastrell. Late-ripening and sun-loving, it thrives in hot, dry climates and lends structure to many southern French and Spanish blends.

**In the glass** — a deeply coloured, muscular wine with blackberry, black pepper, dried herbs and a distinctive gamey, earthy note. Tannins are dense and grippy, acidity moderate, and the body full.

**Where it grows** — it stars in Bandol on France's Mediterranean coast and adds backbone to Châteauneuf-du-Pape and other Rhône blends (the M in GSM). As Monastrell it makes robust, affordable reds across southeastern Spain, and it also does well in California and Australia, often labelled Mataro.

**At the table** — pairs well with braised beef, wild boar, and hearty stews.

**Cellaring** — its firm tannins and structure let the best examples, especially Bandol, age gracefully for well over a decade.

name: Malbec
description:
**Malbec** is a red grape from southwest France, historically tied to Cahors, but it found worldwide fame after taking root in Argentina, which is now its spiritual home.

**In the glass** — a dense, inky wine bursting with plum, blackberry and violet, often lifted by cocoa and a touch of sweet spice from oak. Tannins are plush and velvety, acidity moderate, and the body full and generous.

**Where it grows** — in Cahors it makes a darker, more rustic and tannic wine sometimes called "the black wine." In Argentina's high-altitude Mendoza vineyards it becomes softer, riper and more perfumed, with floral lift from the cool mountain nights. It also appears as a minor blending grape in Bordeaux and grows in Chile and beyond.

**At the table** — the classic match is a char-grilled steak.

**Cellaring** — approachable young, though top Mendoza and Cahors bottlings can age well for ten years or more.

name: Sauvignon Blanc
description:
**Sauvignon Blanc** is a white grape from France's Loire Valley (and a parent of Cabernet Sauvignon) prized for its zesty, aromatic character and refreshing bite.

**In the glass** — pale and bright, with piercing aromas of gooseberry, green apple, freshly cut grass and citrus, sometimes edged with a flinty, mineral or even herbaceous "green" note. High acidity keeps it crisp and lively; the body is light and rarely oaked.

**Where it grows** — Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé give it a stony, mineral elegance; New Zealand's Marlborough turns it into an explosively tropical, passion-fruit-scented style. It also shines in Bordeaux (sometimes blended with Sémillon and barrel-aged), South Africa, Chile and California.

**At the table** — a classic with goat cheese, oysters and fresh salads.

**Cellaring** — almost always best enjoyed young and fresh, within a couple of years, though barrel-fermented Bordeaux versions can develop with time.

name: Nebbiolo
description:
**Nebbiolo** is a red grape from Italy's Piedmont, the noble variety behind Barolo and Barbaresco and one of the world's great age-worthy wines. Its name likely evokes the autumn fog (nebbia) that blankets the Langhe hills at harvest.

**In the glass** — deceptively pale and garnet-hued, yet powerful, with haunting aromas of rose petal, tar, dried cherry, truffle and dried herbs. It combines fierce, drying tannins with searing acidity in a medium body, a hallmark tension that rewards patience.

**Where it grows** — Barolo is fuller and more structured, Barbaresco a touch more perfumed and elegant. It also appears in Gattinara, Ghemme and the Valtellina, but rarely succeeds far from its Piedmontese home.

**At the table** — made for truffle dishes, braised beef and rich risottos.

**Cellaring** — one of the longest-lived reds; the best Barolo needs a decade to soften and can last for decades.

name: Carignan
description:
**Carignan** is a red grape of Spanish origin, traced to Aragón, where it is known as Cariñena. Long grown for volume, old-vine plantings are now prized for concentration and character.

**In the glass** — deeply coloured, with tart red and black berry fruit, dried herbs and a rustic, earthy edge. It is marked by high acidity and firm, sometimes rugged tannins, giving a robust medium-to-full body.

**Where it grows** — it is widespread in southern France's Languedoc-Roussillon, where gnarled old vines yield some of its finest wines, and it plays a supporting role in many Mediterranean blends. In Spain it appears as Cariñena and in Sardinia as Carignano. It is also grown in Chile and California.

**At the table** — good with grilled sausages, lamb and tomato-based stews.

**Cellaring** — old-vine examples can age a decade, but most are best enjoyed within a few years.

name: Zinfandel
description:
**Zinfandel** is a red grape genetically identical to Croatia's Tribidrag (or Crljenak) and to southern Italy's Primitivo, though it became an icon in California.

**In the glass** — a bold, ripe red brimming with jammy blackberry, brambly raspberry, black pepper and sweet baking spice. It often carries high alcohol, moderate tannins and a plush, juicy body, sometimes tipping into raisined, port-like richness when very ripe.

**Where it grows** — California is its heartland, with old-vine plantings in Sonoma, Lodi and the Sierra Foothills giving concentrated, characterful reds; it is also the grape behind sweet, pale "White Zinfandel" rosé. As Primitivo it makes darker, rustic reds in Puglia, and its roots trace back to Croatia.

**At the table** — a natural with barbecue, burgers and smoky grilled meats.

**Cellaring** — usually best in its exuberant youth, though old-vine bottlings can hold for several years.

name: Touriga Nacional
description:
**Touriga Nacional** is a red grape widely regarded as Portugal's finest, native to the Dão and Douro regions and a cornerstone of both Port and premium dry reds.

**In the glass** — intensely coloured and aromatic, offering blackberry, violet, bergamot and a floral, almost perfumed lift. It brings firm tannins, good acidity and a full, concentrated body, giving wines real power and grip.

**Where it grows** — in the steep, schist terraces of the Douro it is central to fortified Port and increasingly to structured table wines, while the Dão produces a more elegant, aromatic style. Naturally low-yielding, it is now planted in small amounts in Australia, South Africa and elsewhere.

**At the table** — excellent with roast game, duck and rich meat dishes.

**Cellaring** — its structure and depth make it very age-worthy, with the best dry and fortified wines lasting many years.

name: Cinsault
description:
**Cinsault** is a red grape long grown in France's Languedoc, valued for its soft, fruity charm and its role in blends and rosés across the Mediterranean.

**In the glass** — a pale-to-medium red with fresh red-cherry and strawberry fruit, a floral hint and gentle spice. It is light-bodied with low, supple tannins and moderate acidity, making for easy, aromatic drinking.

**Where it grows** — it is a traditional blending partner in the southern Rhône and Languedoc, softening firmer grapes like Syrah, Grenache and Mourvèdre, and is a mainstay of Provençal rosé. Heat-tolerant, it also grows in South Africa, where it is a parent of Pinotage, as well as in Lebanon and North Africa.

**At the table** — pairs happily with grilled vegetables, charcuterie and light summer fare.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed young, while its fresh fruit and floral character are at their liveliest.

name: Corvina
description:
**Corvina** is a red grape from Italy's Veneto region, the leading variety behind the wines of Valpolicella, including its famous dried-grape styles.

**In the glass** — typically light-to-medium in colour, with bright sour-cherry and red-berry fruit, a hint of almond and a fresh, slightly bitter twist on the finish. It has high acidity, modest tannins and a light body in its everyday form.

**Where it grows** — it is grown chiefly around Verona, blended with grapes like Rondinella and Molinara. Its true magic emerges when the grapes are dried (appassimento) to make rich, powerful Amarone and sweet Recioto, or partially dried for the fuller Ripasso style.

**At the table** — light Valpolicella suits pizza and pasta, while Amarone stands up to braised beef and aged cheese.

**Cellaring** — fresh versions are best young, but concentrated Amarone can age for well over a decade.

name: Chenin Blanc
description:
**Chenin Blanc** is a versatile white grape from France's Loire Valley, capable of everything from bone-dry to lusciously sweet and sparkling, all underpinned by vibrant acidity.

**In the glass** — expect quince, yellow apple, honey and a distinctive lanolin or wet-wool note, often with a chalky mineral streak. Its hallmark is racy, mouthwatering acidity, which balances styles ranging from crisp and dry to richly honeyed dessert wines.

**Where it grows** — in the Loire it shines in Vouvray, Savennières and Anjou, where botrytis can produce sublime sweet wines. South Africa grows more Chenin than anywhere, historically called Steen, making everything from easy dry whites to serious barrel-aged bottlings; it is also found in California.

**At the table** — dry styles pair with roast chicken and creamy sauces; sweet versions with fruit tarts or blue cheese.

**Cellaring** — its acidity gives remarkable longevity; the finest dry and sweet Loire wines can age for decades.

name: Viognier
description:
**Viognier** is a white grape from the northern Rhône Valley in France, long the signature of the tiny appellation Condrieu and a variety that came close to disappearing before a revival spread it far beyond its Rhône home.

**In the glass** — expect a golden hue and heady aromatics of apricot, peach, honeysuckle and violet, wrapped in a full, almost oily body with soft acidity and a rich, rounded texture.

**Where it grows** — its ancestral home is Condrieu and Château-Grillet in the northern Rhône, where a splash is also sometimes co-fermented with Syrah in Côte-Rôtie. It has since spread widely to the southern Rhône and Languedoc, and to warmer New World zones such as California, Australia and South America, where riper fruit can push the aromatics to exuberant heights.

**At the table** — lovely with roast chicken, mild curries or apricot-glazed pork.

**Cellaring** — generally best enjoyed within a few years while its perfume is fresh, though the finest Condrieu can gain complexity with modest age.

name: Pinot Blanc
description:
**Pinot Blanc** is a white grape most associated with Alsace in France, a colour mutation within the Pinot family and known in German-speaking regions as Weißburgunder or Weisser Burgunder.

**In the glass** — pale and gently aromatic, it offers subtle apple, pear and almond notes, a medium body and fresh but unaggressive acidity, making it one of the more understated and food-friendly whites.

**Where it grows** — Alsace treats it as a versatile everyday white, sometimes blended with Auxerrois. It is widely planted in Germany and Austria as Weißburgunder, in northern Italy as Pinot Bianco, and turns up in central Europe and parts of the New World, where cooler sites keep its delicate freshness intact.

**At the table** — a reliable partner for quiche, seafood, soft cheeses and lighter poultry.

**Cellaring** — usually best drunk young and fresh, though richer, riper examples can hold for a handful of years.

name: Pinot Gris
description:
**Pinot Gris** is a white grape and a greyish-skinned mutation of Pinot Noir, historically at home in Alsace and known around the world as Pinot Grigio in Italy and Grauburgunder in German-speaking countries.

**In the glass** — its style splits sharply by region: rich, spicy and full-bodied with pear, quince and smoky notes in Alsace, versus lighter, crisper and more citrus-driven when made as Italian Pinot Grigio.

**Where it grows** — Alsace produces its most opulent, sometimes off-dry versions, while northern Italy turns out vast quantities of the leaner Pinot Grigio style. It also thrives in Germany, Austria, Oregon, New Zealand and Australia, where producers choose which end of the spectrum to chase.

**At the table** — the crisp style suits antipasti and shellfish; the richer Alsace style stands up to smoked fish, pork and charcuterie.

**Cellaring** — most is best young, but concentrated Alsace bottlings can age gracefully for several years.

name: Rondinella
description:
**Rondinella** is a red grape from the Veneto region of northeast Italy, valued less as a soloist than as a dependable supporting player in the blends of Valpolicella and its powerful cousin Amarone.

**In the glass** — it is fairly light in colour and flavour, contributing red-cherry fruit, gentle floral hints and reliably fresh acidity, with modest tannin and a straightforward, easygoing character.

**Where it grows** — it is grown almost entirely in the Veneto, especially around Verona, where it partners Corvina and Corvinone in Valpolicella, Bardolino, and the dried-grape wines Amarone and Recioto. Its hardiness and generous yields make it a practical vineyard companion rather than a star.

**At the table** — pairs happily with pasta in tomato sauce, pizza and roast poultry.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed young in fresh Valpolicella, though it gains longevity when part of a concentrated Amarone blend.

name: Touriga Franca
description:
**Touriga Franca** is a red grape from the Douro Valley of northern Portugal, one of the most widely planted varieties in the region and a cornerstone of both Port and increasingly ambitious dry reds.

**In the glass** — it brings ripe blackberry and dark-cherry fruit, floral and sometimes rosemary-like hints, supple tannins and good colour, lending elegance and perfume alongside firmer grapes in a blend.

**Where it grows** — its heartland is the Douro, where it is prized for reliability and is often blended with Touriga Nacional and Tinta Roriz. It is also grown across other Portuguese regions and in the neighbouring Dão, valued for balancing power with aromatic lift.

**At the table** — the dry reds suit grilled lamb and hearty stews; Port is a classic match for blue cheese and chocolate.

**Cellaring** — dry Douro reds reward several years in the cellar, and its contribution helps Vintage Port age for decades.

name: Tinta Barroca
description:
**Tinta Barroca** is a red grape from the Douro Valley in northern Portugal, one of the traditional varieties used in Port and Douro red blends, prized for its productivity and deep colour.

**In the glass** — it delivers dark, jammy berry fruit and a soft, fleshy texture, with relatively low acidity and gentle tannins that add sweetness and body to a blend rather than structure.

**Where it grows** — it is grown chiefly in the Douro and Trás-os-Montes, where it is often planted on cooler, higher or north-facing sites because it can struggle in extreme heat. Small plantings exist in South Africa. It is almost always blended alongside grapes such as Touriga Nacional and Touriga Franca.

**At the table** — its blended reds suit grilled meats, sausages and rich stews.

**Cellaring** — it lends early-drinking generosity, and contributes to Ports built to age over the long term.

name: Barbera
description:
**Barbera** is a red grape from the Piedmont region of northwest Italy, long the everyday red of the area and now taken seriously enough to rival its noble neighbour Nebbiolo in quality-minded hands.

**In the glass** — its calling card is bright, mouth-watering acidity paired with deep colour, juicy red- and black-cherry fruit and characteristically soft, low tannins, giving a lively, food-friendly character.

**Where it grows** — Piedmont is its home, notably in Barbera d'Asti and Barbera d'Alba, ranging from fresh unoaked styles to richer, barrel-aged versions. It is planted across much of Italy and has a strong following in California, Argentina and Australia, where warmth softens its natural acidity.

**At the table** — its acidity makes it a natural with tomato-based pasta, pizza, salami and roast meats.

**Cellaring** — most is delicious young, while oak-aged, concentrated examples can improve over five to ten years.

name: Sémillon
description:
**Sémillon** is a white grape from Bordeaux in France, famous as the backbone of the world's greatest sweet wines and an increasingly respected component of fine dry whites.

**In the glass** — when dry it is fuller-bodied and relatively low in acidity, showing lemon, waxy lanolin and hints of honey; when affected by noble rot it turns lusciously sweet, with apricot, marmalade and botrytis richness.

**Where it grows** — its heartland is Bordeaux, where it stars in the sweet wines of Sauternes and Barsac and blends with Sauvignon Blanc for dry whites. It is central to Australia's Hunter Valley, which makes remarkable long-lived dry styles, and is also grown in South Africa and elsewhere.

**At the table** — dry Sémillon suits fish and poultry, while the sweet wines are classic with foie gras and blue cheese.

**Cellaring** — both styles age beautifully; Sauternes and Hunter Sémillon can evolve gracefully for many decades.

name: Nero d'Avola
description:
**Nero d'Avola** is a red grape from Sicily, the island's most important and widely planted dark variety, whose name references the town of Avola in the southeast.

**In the glass** — it typically shows deep colour, ripe black cherry and plum fruit, a warming, full-bodied palate and moderate tannins, often with a savoury, slightly peppery edge that reflects its sun-drenched origins.

**Where it grows** — Sicily is its home, from the traditional heartland around the southeastern corner to plantings across the island, where styles range from soft and fruity everyday reds to structured, ambitious bottlings, sometimes blended with the lighter Frappato. It is largely a Sicilian speciality with only limited plantings elsewhere.

**At the table** — a good match for grilled meats, tomato-rich pasta and aubergine dishes.

**Cellaring** — approachable young, though the more serious, concentrated examples can develop well over several years.

name: Gamay
description:
**Gamay** is a red grape best known as the sole variety of Beaujolais in eastern France, a cheerful, juicy wine that ranges from simple and fruity to surprisingly serious.

**In the glass** — it is typically light to medium-bodied with a bright ruby colour, fresh red-berry and cherry fruit, sometimes a banana or bubblegum note in carbonic styles, soft tannins and lively acidity.

**Where it grows** — Beaujolais is its heartland, from easy Beaujolais Nouveau to the more structured and age-worthy Crus such as Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent. It is also grown in the Loire, Switzerland (often blended), and pockets of the New World, where cool sites preserve its refreshing character.

**At the table** — versatile and lightly chilled, it flatters charcuterie, roast chicken and many cheeses.

**Cellaring** — most is made for early drinking, but the top Cru Beaujolais can age and grow more Pinot-like over a decade.

name: Corvinone
description:
**Corvinone** is a red grape from the Veneto region of northeast Italy, long confused with Corvina but now recognised as a distinct variety and an important contributor to the wines of the Verona hills.

**In the glass** — it offers red-cherry and dried-fruit character with firm structure, good acidity and moderate tannin, and its large berries partly dry particularly well, concentrating flavour and sweetness.

**Where it grows** — it is grown almost exclusively in the Veneto, especially in Valpolicella, where it is blended with Corvina and Rondinella for Valpolicella, Bardolino, and the appassimento wines Amarone and Recioto made from grapes dried after harvest.

**At the table** — its blends suit braised meats, game and aged hard cheeses.

**Cellaring** — light Valpolicella is best young, but its role in Amarone yields powerful wines that can age for many years.

name: Graciano
description:
**Graciano** is a red grape from Spain's Rioja region, most often used in small proportions to add backbone and lift to blends built around Tempranillo. Long overlooked because it ripens late and yields stingily, it has enjoyed a quiet revival among growers chasing complexity.

**In the glass** — deeply coloured and marked by bright, high acidity, firm tannin and dark aromas of blackberry, violet and dried herbs, with a savoury, almost peppery edge. It brings freshness and grip rather than plush fruit.

**Where it grows** — its heartland is Rioja and neighbouring Navarra, where it seasons Tempranillo-led wines, and it appears under the name Morrastel and as a varietal bottling from a handful of ambitious estates. Australia and California also grow small plots.

**At the table** — excellent with roast lamb, grilled red meats or aged sheep's-milk cheese.

**Cellaring** — its acidity and tannin make it a good keeper, and quality bottlings can improve for a decade or more.

name: Montepulciano
description:
**Montepulciano** is a red grape from central and southern Italy, most closely tied to the Abruzzo region on the Adriatic coast. It is one of Italy's most widely planted reds and should not be confused with the Tuscan town of Montepulciano, whose wines are made from Sangiovese.

**In the glass** — deeply coloured, generous and juicy, with ripe black cherry and plum fruit, gentle spice, moderate acidity and soft, ample tannins that make it approachable young. Styles range from easy everyday reds to more concentrated, structured wines.

**Where it grows** — Abruzzo is its home, where Montepulciano d'Abruzzo covers a wide quality spectrum; it is also important in the Marche, Molise and Puglia. Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo is a deep-hued rosé made from the same grape.

**At the table** — a natural match for tomato-based pasta, pizza and grilled sausages.

**Cellaring** — most is made for early drinking, though top single-estate versions can age gracefully for ten years or so.

name: Glera
description:
**Glera** is a white grape from north-eastern Italy, grown across the Veneto and Friuli, and it is the variety behind Prosecco. The grape was in fact renamed Glera so that "Prosecco" could be protected as a place-based name rather than a grape name.

**In the glass** — light, crisp and fragrant, with delicate aromas of green apple, pear, white blossom and a touch of citrus, brisk acidity and a soft, frothy texture in sparkling form. It is charming and uncomplicated rather than deep.

**Where it grows** — its home is the hills of Conegliano and Valdobbiadene and the surrounding plains of the Veneto and Friuli, where it is chiefly made into sparkling wine by the tank method. Small amounts of still and lightly fizzy wine are also produced.

**At the table** — a lovely aperitif, and good with light antipasti, seafood or fresh fruit.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed young and fresh, ideally within a year or two of release.

name: Tinto Cão
description:
**Tinto Cão** is a red grape native to Portugal's Douro Valley, counted among the classic varieties permitted for Port and increasingly valued for dry table wines. Its name translates roughly as "red dog," and it is prized for the finesse and freshness it lends to blends.

**In the glass** — it tends toward elegance rather than power, offering fragrant red fruit, floral notes and fine spice, with firm acidity and refined tannins that give lift and length.

**Where it grows** — the Douro is its stronghold, both for fortified Port and for the region's growing range of dry reds, and it is also planted more modestly in the Dão. Because it ripens late and yields little, plantings remain limited.

**At the table** — pairs well with roasted meats, game and hearty stews.

**Cellaring** — its structure and acidity make it a fine component for long-lived wines, contributing to blends built to age for many years.

name: Roussanne
description:
**Roussanne** is a white grape from France's northern Rhône, often partnered with Marsanne to make some of the region's most distinguished whites. Its name is thought to nod to the russet tint the ripe berries take on.

**In the glass** — aromatic and refined, showing pear, quince, honeysuckle, herbal tea and a nutty note, with vibrant acidity and an elegant, structured palate that can gain weight and complexity with age.

**Where it grows** — it is central to the northern Rhône appellations such as Hermitage, Crozes-Hermitage and Saint-Joseph, and features in the whites of Châteauneuf-du-Pape further south. It has also spread to the Languedoc, California, Australia and beyond, often in Rhône-style blends.

**At the table** — good with roast poultry, richer fish dishes and creamy soft cheeses.

**Cellaring** — unusually age-worthy for a white, the best examples develop honeyed, nutty complexity over five to ten years or more.

name: Gewürztraminer
description:
**Gewürztraminer** is a pink-skinned white grape whose roots trace to the village of Tramin in Italy's Alto Adige, a mutation of the older Traminer family. Its name literally means "spiced Traminer," a fitting label for one of the most instantly recognisable of all white wines.

**In the glass** — richly perfumed with lychee, rose petal, ginger and exotic spice, it is typically full-bodied, low in acidity and deep golden in colour, with an oily texture and styles running from dry to lusciously sweet.

**Where it grows** — Alsace in France is its most celebrated home, alongside its Alto Adige birthplace; it also thrives in Germany, Austria, New Zealand and cooler pockets of North America.

**At the table** — a classic foil for spicy Asian dishes, and superb with pungent cheeses like Munster and with foie gras.

**Cellaring** — dry versions drink well young but can hold several years, while sweet late-harvest bottlings age beautifully for decades.

name: Petite Sirah
description:
**Petite Sirah** is a red grape that originated in France as Durif, a cross of Syrah and the obscure Peloursin, though it found its lasting fame in California and Australia. Despite the name, it is a distinct variety and not simply a small-berried Syrah.

**In the glass** — inky and dark, it delivers powerful blackberry and plum fruit, black pepper and dark chocolate, with high tannin, robust structure and full body. It is one of the most deeply coloured of all red wines.

**Where it grows** — California is its true home today, both as a bold varietal and as a blending grape to add colour and grip; it is also grown in Australia (where the name Durif persists), Israel and elsewhere.

**At the table** — made for grilled steak, barbecue and rich braises.

**Cellaring** — its tannin and depth reward patience, and serious examples can develop for a decade or more.

name: Vermentino
description:
**Vermentino** is a white grape of the Mediterranean coast, closely identified with Italy's Liguria and the island of Sardinia, and known in southern France as Rolle. It makes some of the most refreshing, sea-breezy whites of the region.

**In the glass** — bright and zesty, showing citrus, green apple, white flowers and a distinctive herbal, saline note, with crisp acidity, light-to-medium body and often a faintly bitter, almond-tinged finish.

**Where it grows** — its strongholds are Sardinia and the Ligurian coast in Italy, and Corsica and Provence in France, where as Rolle it lends fragrance to blends. It is grown in Tuscany, the Languedoc and increasingly in Australia and California.

**At the table** — a natural partner for grilled fish, shellfish and other seafood.

**Cellaring** — generally best enjoyed young and fresh, within a couple of years, though a few structured versions can hold longer.

name: Muscadelle
description:
**Muscadelle** is a white grape from the Bordeaux region of France, traditionally used as a minor blending partner to Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc. Despite the name, it is unrelated to the Muscat family, though it shares a lightly grapey perfume.

**In the glass** — floral and delicately aromatic, with notes of grape, honeysuckle and orchard fruit, generally soft and low in acidity, adding fragrance rather than backbone to a blend.

**Where it grows** — its home is Bordeaux and the wider south-west of France, where it seasons both dry and sweet whites such as those of Sauternes. It also has a notable second life in Australia, where under the old name Tokay it is used for the luscious fortified wines of Rutherglen.

**At the table** — dry styles suit light fish and salads, while sweet versions pair with fruit desserts.

**Cellaring** — dry wines are best drunk young, but the fortified and sweet styles age remarkably well.

name: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains
description:
**Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains** is a white grape of ancient Mediterranean origin, regarded as the oldest and finest member of the sprawling Muscat family. Known by a host of names — Moscato Bianco, Muscat de Frontignan, Sárgamuskotály and Muskateller among them — it is prized for its unmistakable perfume.

**In the glass** — intensely aromatic with orange blossom, grape, rose and musk, it is made in every style from dry to sparkling to richly sweet, usually light-bodied with fresh acidity and a genuinely grapey flavour.

**Where it grows** — with roots in the ancient Mediterranean, it now flourishes across Italy (as Moscato Bianco, notably in Asti), southern France (for the sweet Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise and Frontignan), Greece, Austria, Hungary and beyond.

**At the table** — sweet styles shine with fruit tarts and creamy desserts; dry versions suit aperitifs.

**Cellaring** — most are made to enjoy young for their fragrance, though the finest sweet fortified versions can age for many years.

name: Aglianico
description:
**Aglianico** is a noble red grape of southern Italy, centred on the regions of Campania and Basilicata, and often called the "Barolo of the south" for its power and longevity. It is an ancient variety of the volcanic hills of the Mezzogiorno.

**In the glass** — deeply coloured and formidably structured, it offers dark plum and black cherry, tar, leather, dried herbs and smoke, with high acidity and firm, grippy tannins that demand time to soften.

**Where it grows** — its two great expressions are Taurasi in Campania and Aglianico del Vulture in Basilicata, both grown on volcanic soils; it is also planted across Puglia, Molise and increasingly in the New World.

**At the table** — superb with braised and roasted red meats, game and aged hard cheeses.

**Cellaring** — one of Italy's most age-worthy reds, the best examples need years to open and can develop for two decades or more.

name: Grenache Blanc
description:
**Grenache Blanc** is a white grape, the pale-berried cousin of red Grenache, with roots in northern Spain, where it goes by Garnacha Blanca. It is one of the workhorse white varieties of the warm Mediterranean south.

**In the glass** — expect a full-bodied, generous wine with modest acidity, flavours leaning toward green apple, fennel, dried herbs and a faintly nutty richness. Its low aromatic intensity is offset by weight and a rounded, oily texture.

**Where it grows** — it is at home across the southern Rhône, Languedoc-Roussillon and Catalonia, usually blended with partners like Roussanne, Marsanne, Clairette or Viognier that lend acidity and perfume. In cooler sites or with careful winemaking it stays fresh; in hot vintages it can turn broad and heady.

**At the table** — lovely with roast chicken, grilled fish or vegetable dishes rich in olive oil.

**Cellaring** — most versions are best young, though barrel-aged or top southern Rhône whites can develop nicely over several years.

name: Macabeo
description:
**Macabeo** is a white grape from Spain, prominent in both Rioja and Catalonia, where it is also called Viura and Macabeu. It is one of the most planted white varieties in Spain and a cornerstone of Cava.

**In the glass** — it tends to be light to medium-bodied and gently aromatic, offering green apple, pear, white blossom and a subtle almond note, with fresh acidity and a clean finish. Young examples are crisp and easygoing.

**Where it grows** — in Rioja it is the backbone of white blends, sometimes fermented or aged in oak for a richer style; in Penedès and neighbouring Catalan zones it is the leading grape in the traditional-method sparkling Cava, usually alongside Xarel-lo and Parellada.

**At the table** — a natural match for tapas, seafood, and lighter poultry dishes.

**Cellaring** — generally made to be drunk young and fresh, though barrel-aged Rioja whites can reward a few years in the cellar.

name: Frappato
description:
**Frappato** is a red grape native to Sicily, especially the island's south-eastern corner around Vittoria. It is prized for producing bright, fragrant wines that feel almost weightless.

**In the glass** — it pours a light, translucent ruby and bursts with red cherry, wild strawberry and floral notes, sometimes a whisper of pepper. The palate is fresh and juicy, with high acidity, soft tannins and a light body that invites a chill.

**Where it grows** — its heartland is Sicily, where it stars in varietal bottlings and, most famously, is blended with Nero d'Avola to make Cerasuolo di Vittoria, the island's only DOCG. Warm coastal sites give ripeness while the grape keeps its perfume and lift.

**At the table** — serve lightly chilled with grilled fish, tomato-based pasta, or roasted vegetables.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed young while its aromatics and freshness are at their peak.

name: Grüner Veltliner
description:
**Grüner Veltliner** is a white grape and Austria's signature variety, most associated with Lower Austria (Niederösterreich). It ranges from crisp everyday wines to serious, age-worthy bottlings.

**In the glass** — its hallmark is a savoury tension between citrus and green apple, a peppery, radish-like spice, and a mineral streak. Bright acidity keeps it lively, while riper examples gain stone-fruit weight and a rounder body.

**Where it grows** — the great sites cluster along the Danube in the Wachau, Kamptal and Kremstal, where terraced vineyards yield concentrated, structured wines. It is also widely grown across Austria and neighbouring parts of Central Europe, with lighter, zesty styles at the entry level.

**At the table** — famously versatile, it handles tricky partners like asparagus, artichokes and Wiener schnitzel with ease.

**Cellaring** — simple versions shine young, but top single-vineyard wines can age gracefully for a decade or more, gaining honeyed depth.

name: Marsanne
description:
**Marsanne** is a white grape from the northern Rhône Valley of France, often paired with Roussanne in the region's classic white blends. It gives weighty, textural wines built more on body than on overt perfume.

**In the glass** — it is typically full-bodied and rich, with flavours of ripe pear, quince, almond and honeysuckle, and a waxy, sometimes oily texture. Acidity runs low to moderate, so the appeal lies in its breadth and depth.

**Where it grows** — its home appellations are Hermitage, Crozes-Hermitage and Saint-Joseph, and it spreads through the southern Rhône and Languedoc. It has also found success in Australia and California, where warm sites amplify its generous character.

**At the table** — pairs well with roast poultry, creamy fish dishes and mild soft cheeses.

**Cellaring** — while approachable young, the finest northern Rhône examples can age for many years, developing marzipan and honeyed complexity.

name: Nerello Mascalese
description:
**Nerello Mascalese** is a red grape from Sicily, most celebrated on the volcanic slopes of Mount Etna. It has become one of Italy's most sought-after varieties for its elegance and sense of place.

**In the glass** — it shows a pale to medium ruby colour and aromas of red cherry, dried herbs, orange peel and a smoky, mineral edge. The palate is refined and structured, with firm tannins, high acidity and a graceful, almost Burgundian or Nebbiolo-like poise.

**Where it grows** — its spiritual home is Etna, where high-altitude vineyards on mineral-rich volcanic soils and old vines produce Etna Rosso, often blended with a little Nerello Cappuccio. Site and elevation strongly shape its expression.

**At the table** — enjoy with roasted meats, mushroom dishes, or aged cheeses.

**Cellaring** — the best examples are genuinely age-worthy, evolving over a decade or more toward savoury, tertiary complexity.

name: Dolcetto
description:
**Dolcetto** is a red grape from Piedmont in north-west Italy, valued as the region's everyday red alongside its more austere neighbours Barbera and Nebbiolo. Its name hints at "little sweet one," a reference to the grape rather than the wine, which is dry.

**In the glass** — it is deeply coloured, with aromas of black cherry, plum, licorice and a dusting of almond bitterness on the finish. The palate is soft and fruity, with moderate to firm tannins, relatively low acidity and an approachable, rounded body.

**Where it grows** — its heartland is Piedmont, with named zones such as Dolcetto d'Alba, Dogliani and Dolcetto di Diano d'Alba. It thrives in cooler, higher sites where the later-ripening Nebbiolo struggles.

**At the table** — a friendly partner for pizza, cured meats, and everyday pasta.

**Cellaring** — meant to be drunk young, within a few years, while its fruit is fresh.

name: Clairette
description:
**Clairette** is a white grape long grown in the south of France, including the southern Rhône and the wider Mediterranean coast. It is a traditional blending grape that has been part of the region's whites for centuries.

**In the glass** — it offers a medium to full body with gentle aromas of white flowers, apple, fennel and a touch of citrus, sometimes a faintly bitter, herbal finish. Acidity is on the lower side, so it is often blended with fresher partners for balance.

**Where it grows** — it appears across the southern Rhône, Languedoc and Provence, both in still white blends and in the historic sparkling wine Clairette de Die. It is prone to oxidation, which shapes how it is handled in the cellar.

**At the table** — pairs nicely with Provençal vegetable dishes, grilled fish and herbed poultry.

**Cellaring** — generally best enjoyed young while its delicate florals and freshness remain.

name: Molinara
description:
**Molinara** is a red grape from the Veneto region of north-east Italy, known chiefly as a supporting player in the wines of the Valpolicella area. Its name is linked to the dusty, floury bloom on its ripe berries.

**In the glass** — it is light in colour and body, giving fresh red-fruit and cranberry notes with a savoury, slightly saline lift. High acidity and gentle tannins make it more about brightness than power.

**Where it grows** — it is a traditional component of Valpolicella and Bardolino blends, alongside Corvina and Rondinella, where it adds acidity and freshness. Its role has diminished over time as growers favour the more concentrated Corvina, but it remains part of the classic recipe.

**At the table** — good with lighter meat dishes, charcuterie and tomato-based pasta.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed young, as its charm lies in freshness rather than aging potential.

name: Xarel-lo
description:
**Xarel-lo** is a white grape from Catalonia in Spain, centred on the Penedès region, where it is also known as Pansa Blanca. It is one of the three classic grapes of traditional-method Cava and increasingly prized on its own.

**In the glass** — it delivers more structure and character than many of its blending partners, with green apple, pear, fennel and a distinctive earthy, herbal note, plus firm acidity and a hint of grip. This backbone is what makes it valuable in sparkling blends.

**Where it grows** — its home is Penedès and surrounding Catalan zones, where it anchors Cava alongside Macabeo and Parellada, and appears as a serious, sometimes oak-aged still white. Coastal Mediterranean conditions suit it well.

**At the table** — pairs with seafood, cured ham, and grilled vegetables.

**Cellaring** — fresh styles drink young, but its acidity and structure allow the best still and sparkling wines to age well for several years.

name: Alicante Bouschet
description:
**Alicante Bouschet** is a red grape created in nineteenth-century France, in the Languedoc lineage of the Bouschet breeders. It is a teinturier, meaning its flesh and juice are red rather than clear, which is unusual among wine grapes.

**In the glass** — it produces intensely dark, inky wines with deep purple hues and flavours of blackberry, plum and dark chocolate, backed by robust tannins and full body. Its main historic use was to deepen colour in blends.

**Where it grows** — from its French origins it spread widely to Iberia, especially Portugal's Alentejo, as well as Spain, North Africa and California, thriving in warm climates. In the Alentejo it has become a respected varietal wine in its own right, not just a blending grape.

**At the table** — stands up to grilled red meats, stews and hearty roasts.

**Cellaring** — the more serious examples can age for several years, softening their tannic frame.

name: Albariño
description:
**Albariño** is a white grape from the damp, Atlantic-facing corner of northwest Spain, where it is the signature variety of Rías Baixas in Galicia and the source of some of the country's most refreshing whites.

**In the glass** — expect a pale, bright wine with a lift of citrus, white peach, apricot and a saline, sea-breeze note, carried on crisp, mouth-watering acidity and a light-to-medium body that often feels almost tactile in its freshness.

**Where it grows** — its heartland is Galicia, and just across the border in Portugal's Vinho Verde it goes by Alvarinho, where it can feel a touch riper. It has also been picked up by growers in California, Oregon and elsewhere chasing its zippy, aromatic style.

**At the table** — a natural partner for shellfish, grilled sardines and other seafood.

**Cellaring** — generally best enjoyed young and fresh, though the more serious, lees-aged examples can gain texture over a few years.

name: Aligoté
description:
**Aligoté** is a white grape from Burgundy in eastern France, long overshadowed by Chardonnay but valued for its bracing, no-frills freshness and its role in the classic Kir cocktail.

**In the glass** — it tends toward a lean, high-acid style with green apple, lemon, white flowers and a chalky, sometimes slightly herbal edge, usually light-bodied and unoaked.

**Where it grows** — its home is the Burgundian side-roads, with its own appellation at Bouzeron and plantings scattered across the Côte and the Hautes-Côtes. It is also grown widely in Eastern Europe and the former Soviet countries, and has a small following among growers elsewhere who prize its zesty acidity.

**At the table** — good with oysters, snails in garlic butter, and simple goat cheese.

**Cellaring** — mostly made to drink young, though old-vine bottlings from top sites can develop attractively over several years.

name: Carmenère
description:
**Carmenère** is a red grape that originated in Bordeaux, where it was once part of the blend before phylloxera and difficult ripening pushed it to the margins; today it thrives in Chile, which has adopted it as a signature variety.

**In the glass** — it gives a deep, purple-red wine with blackberry, plum, and a distinctive savoury streak of green pepper, tomato leaf, soy and spice, with soft-to-medium tannins and moderate acidity.

**Where it grows** — Chile is now its stronghold, especially the warm valleys around Colchagua and Maipo where full ripeness tames the herbaceous edge. Smaller amounts survive in Bordeaux and appear in Italy's northeast and parts of China.

**At the table** — a fine match for grilled red meats, peppered steak and hearty stews.

**Cellaring** — approachable young, but the more structured examples reward five to ten years in the cellar.

name: Arinto
description:
**Arinto** is a white grape from Portugal, most closely associated with the small Bucelas region near Lisbon, and prized above all for its firm, long-lasting acidity.

**In the glass** — it shows lemon and green apple with mineral and sometimes waxy or honeyed notes, framed by crisp acidity and a fairly light, focused body.

**Where it grows** — beyond its Bucelas home it is planted across much of central and southern Portugal, including the Vinho Verde area and the Alentejo, where it is often blended in to bring freshness and backbone to warmer-climate whites.

**At the table** — pairs well with grilled fish, salt cod and seafood rice.

**Cellaring** — usually enjoyable young, though its natural acidity lets good examples age gracefully for a decade or more, gaining honeyed, toasty complexity.

name: Negroamaro
description:
**Negroamaro** is a red grape of southern Italy, deeply rooted in Puglia's sun-baked heel, where it has long been one of the workhorse varieties of the region.

**In the glass** — it produces dark, full-bodied wines with ripe black cherry and plum, a warming note of dried herbs and spice, and often a faintly bitter, savoury finish that echoes its name, with soft tannins and moderate acidity.

**Where it grows** — it is almost entirely a Puglian speciality, central to appellations such as Salice Salentino and widespread across the Salento peninsula, frequently blended with the perfumed Malvasia Nera.

**At the table** — excellent with grilled lamb, tomato-rich pasta and aged cheeses.

**Cellaring** — enjoyable in its youth for its generous fruit, though the more concentrated bottlings can hold and improve over several years.

name: Vidal Blanc
description:
**Vidal Blanc** is a white hybrid grape bred in France, crossing a Vitis vinifera parent with a hardy North American hybrid, which gives it the winter toughness that made it a star of cold-climate winemaking.

**In the glass** — it is highly aromatic, offering pineapple, apricot, grapefruit and floral notes, and because it retains acidity even when very ripe it can produce anything from crisp dry whites to lusciously sweet dessert wines.

**Where it grows** — it is most famous in Canada, especially Ontario and the Niagara Peninsula, where its thick skins and hardiness make it ideal for icewine. It is also grown across the northeastern United States and other continental, frost-prone regions.

**At the table** — sweet versions shine with fruit tarts and blue cheese; dry ones suit spicy Asian dishes.

**Cellaring** — dry styles are best young, while the sweet icewines can age for many years.

name: Savagnin
description:
**Savagnin** is a white grape from the Jura region of eastern France, best known as the grape behind the region's remarkable oxidative wines.

**In the glass** — in its dramatic *vin jaune* form, aged for years under a veil of yeast, it develops intense curry, walnut, dried apple and bruised-fruit aromas with a bone-dry, almost sherry-like intensity. Made in a more conventional, protected style it is fresher and more floral, with firm acidity.

**Where it grows** — the Jura is its heartland, where it stars in Château-Chalon and other vin jaune appellations. It is genetically linked to the wider Traminer family and appears under various names across Central Europe and increasingly among niche growers elsewhere.

**At the table** — vin jaune is a classic with Comté cheese and chicken in cream sauce.

**Cellaring** — vin jaune is famously long-lived, keeping for decades; fresher styles are best drunk younger.

name: Muscat
description:
**Muscat** is a white grape, or rather a large and ancient family of related varieties grown around the Mediterranean and far beyond, unmistakable for its intensely grapey, floral perfume — one of the few grapes whose wine actually smells of fresh grapes.

**In the glass** — expect exuberant aromas of orange blossom, rose, ripe grape and citrus, in styles ranging from bone-dry to gently sparkling to richly sweet and fortified.

**Where it grows** — the finest, Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, features in France's Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise, Italy's Asti, Greece's Samos and Australia's dark fortified Rutherglen Muscats. Muscat of Alexandria and other family members are planted widely across warm regions worldwide.

**At the table** — sweet Muscats are delightful with fruit desserts and pastries.

**Cellaring** — dry and lightly sparkling styles are best young; the fortified and richly sweet versions can age for decades.

name: Pinotage
description:
**Pinotage** is a red grape created in South Africa in 1925 by crossing Pinot Noir with Cinsault, and it has become the country's distinctive homegrown signature variety.

**In the glass** — it yields deeply coloured wines with dark plum, blackberry and banana notes, often with a smoky, earthy or savoury character, medium-to-full body and firm but ripe tannins.

**Where it grows** — it is overwhelmingly a South African speciality, planted across the Cape from Stellenbosch to Swartland, made in styles that span easy, juicy "coffee Pinotage" to serious, age-worthy reds and even rosé. Small plantings exist in a handful of other New World countries.

**At the table** — a great match for barbecue, grilled sausages and game.

**Cellaring** — lighter versions are best young, but the more structured bottlings can develop well over five to ten years.

name: Godello
description:
**Godello** is a white grape from northwest Spain, native to Galicia and especially the Valdeorras area, where it was rescued from near-extinction in the twentieth century to become one of the region's most prized whites; it is also known as Gouveio in Portugal.

**In the glass** — it offers pear, green apple, citrus and stone fruit with a mineral, sometimes slightly saline edge, medium body, fresh acidity and a naturally rich texture that responds well to lees-ageing and restrained oak.

**Where it grows** — Valdeorras is its benchmark home, with plantings across Galicia and neighbouring León, while as Gouveio it contributes to whites and even Port blends in Portugal's Douro.

**At the table** — lovely with grilled fish, seafood and poultry.

**Cellaring** — enjoyable young, but the more textured, barrel-aged examples can improve and deepen over several years.

name: Silvaner
description:
**Silvaner** is a white grape that arose as a natural crossing with roots in Austria, though it became most closely associated with German winemaking, where it is valued for its gentle, food-friendly character.

**In the glass** — it is typically understated and subtly aromatic, showing green apple, pear, fresh herbs and a distinct earthy or mineral note, with medium acidity and a soft, rounded body that lets terroir speak.

**Where it grows** — Germany is its stronghold, especially Franken, where it produces some of its most characterful, mineral wines, and Rheinhessen. It is also grown in Alsace as Sylvaner and in parts of Central Europe and northern Italy's Alto Adige.

**At the table** — a versatile companion to asparagus, freshwater fish and light vegetable dishes.

**Cellaring** — mostly made to drink young and fresh, though top Franken examples can age gracefully for several years.

name: Parellada
description:
**Parellada** is a white grape from Catalonia in north-eastern Spain, best known as one of the three classic partners — alongside Macabeo and Xarel·lo — in traditional-method Cava.

**In the glass** — Pale and delicate, it offers gentle green-apple, pear and white-flower aromas with a hint of citrus. On the palate it is light-bodied and fresh, with bright acidity and a soft, unassuming finish, contributing finesse and lift rather than power.

**Where it grows** — It is very much a Catalan speciality, planted mainly in the Penedès, where it favours cooler, higher-altitude sites that preserve its acidity and floral perfume. It appears both in sparkling Cava and in light, easy still whites.

**At the table** — Lovely as an aperitif or with light seafood, salads and fresh cheeses.

**Cellaring** — Generally best enjoyed young and fresh, while its delicate aromatics and crisp acidity are at their peak.

name: Tannat
description:
**Tannat** is a red grape from south-west France, historically at home in Madiran, and today just as famous as the signature red of Uruguay. As its name hints, it is one of the most tannic varieties in the wine world.

**In the glass** — Deeply coloured and full-bodied, it shows blackberry, plum, liquorice and smoky, earthy notes, framed by firm acidity and a formidable grip of tannin that softens with time or careful winemaking.

**Where it grows** — In Madiran and the wider Gascony region it makes dense, structured reds, while in Uruguay it produces a slightly rounder, more approachable style that has become a national calling card. It is also grown in Argentina, Brazil and parts of the USA.

**At the table** — A natural match for hearty meat dishes such as cassoulet, lamb or grilled steak.

**Cellaring** — Its tannin and structure reward patience; good examples age well over many years, mellowing and gaining complexity.

name: Baco Noir
description:
**Baco Noir** is a red hybrid grape created in France by François Baco, crossing a Vitis vinifera variety with hardy American vine stock, and it has since found a home largely in North America.

**In the glass** — It tends to be deeply coloured with bright, high acidity and flavours of dark berries, plum and a touch of smoke or earth, usually with light-to-moderate tannin.

**Where it grows** — Prized for its cold-hardiness and disease resistance, it is grown in cooler climates such as Canada (notably Ontario), New York State and Oregon, where it ripens reliably where classic European varieties can struggle.

**At the table** — Its lively acidity suits roasted meats, sausages and tomato-based dishes.

**Cellaring** — Most versions are made for early, everyday drinking, though some fuller, oak-aged examples can hold for a handful of years.

name: Muscat of Alexandria
description:
**Muscat of Alexandria** is an ancient white grape from the eastern Mediterranean, one of the oldest cultivated varieties and a member of the wide-ranging Muscat family. It is known as Zibibbo in Sicily and, when fortified in Portugal, as Moscatel de Setúbal.

**In the glass** — Intensely aromatic, it bursts with orange blossom, honey, grape and candied-citrus scents. Depending on style it ranges from dry and floral to lusciously sweet, generally with modest acidity and a rich, grapey palate.

**Where it grows** — It thrives in warm climates around the Mediterranean and beyond — Greece, Italy (especially Pantelleria), Spain, Portugal, North Africa and Australia — making everything from dry table wines to raisined dessert and fortified wines.

**At the table** — Sweet versions shine with fruit tarts, blue cheese or on their own as dessert.

**Cellaring** — Dry styles are best young, while concentrated sweet and fortified wines can age gracefully for decades.

name: Blaufränkisch
description:
**Blaufränkisch** is a red grape most associated with Austria, especially the Burgenland region, and is also widely grown across Central Europe, where it goes by names such as Lemberger in Germany and Kékfrankos in Hungary.

**In the glass** — It is medium to full-bodied with a deep colour, showing dark cherry and blackberry fruit alongside a distinctive spicy, peppery character and often an earthy, mineral edge. Bright acidity and firm tannins give it real structure.

**Where it grows** — Burgenland is its heartland, but it flourishes throughout Hungary, Germany and neighbouring countries, ranging from juicy, fruit-forward styles to serious, oak-aged, age-worthy reds.

**At the table** — Its acidity and spice pair well with roast pork, game and paprika-spiced dishes.

**Cellaring** — Structured examples can develop beautifully over five to ten years or more, while lighter versions are enjoyable young.

name: Counoise
description:
**Counoise** is a red grape of the southern Rhône in France, best known as a supporting player in blends such as Châteauneuf-du-Pape rather than as a solo star.

**In the glass** — It is typically light to medium-bodied with a bright, peppery, spicy character, red-fruit flavours and lively acidity. Its gentle tannins and freshness add lift, perfume and a lightness of touch to the blends it joins.

**Where it grows** — Its home is the southern Rhône, where it is grown in modest quantities alongside Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre. It has also gained a small following among Rhône-inspired producers in California and elsewhere.

**At the table** — Its spice and acidity suit grilled vegetables, poultry and lightly herbed meat dishes.

**Cellaring** — Generally valued for the freshness it brings young, though it can add nuance to blends built for medium-term ageing.

name: Zweigelt
description:
**Zweigelt** is a red grape bred in Austria in 1922 by crossing St. Laurent with Blaufränkisch, and it has become the country's most widely planted red variety.

**In the glass** — It offers juicy, vibrant red-cherry and berry fruit, often with a hint of spice, medium body, soft-to-moderate tannins and refreshing acidity. Its charm lies in approachable, easygoing fruitiness.

**Where it grows** — It is planted across Austria's wine regions, from Burgenland to the Danube areas, making everything from light, chillable everyday reds to a smaller number of richer, oak-aged, more serious bottlings.

**At the table** — A versatile food wine that partners well with roast chicken, charcuterie, schnitzel and lighter meat dishes.

**Cellaring** — Most is meant for early, cheerful drinking, though ambitious, concentrated examples can hold and improve over several years.

name: Trebbiano Toscano
description:
**Trebbiano Toscano** is a white grape long grown in Tuscany and across central Italy, and one of the world's most planted whites; in France it is known as Ugni Blanc and forms the base of Cognac and Armagnac.

**In the glass** — It is typically light-bodied and fairly neutral, with subtle lemon, green-apple and floral notes, its defining feature being high, refreshing acidity and a crisp, clean finish.

**Where it grows** — Widespread throughout central Italy, it appears in many everyday whites and in Tuscany contributes to the traditional sweet Vin Santo. Its high acidity also makes it ideal for distillation into brandy in France and elsewhere.

**At the table** — Its brightness works well with simple seafood, antipasti and fried dishes.

**Cellaring** — Dry versions are best drunk young and fresh, while the sweet Vin Santo styles can age for years.

name: Castelão
description:
**Castelão** is a red grape from southern Portugal, particularly associated with the Setúbal Peninsula and Palmela, and one of the more widely planted red varieties in the country's warmer south. It also goes by the name Periquita.

**In the glass** — It is medium-bodied with red and dark berry fruit, often accompanied by earthy, spicy and slightly gamey notes as it ages, with fresh acidity and moderate, sometimes firm tannins.

**Where it grows** — It is grown across southern and central Portugal, from the sandy soils of the Setúbal area to the Alentejo and beyond, producing a range of styles from bright, everyday reds to more structured wines.

**At the table** — A good companion to grilled meats, roast pork and rustic Portuguese stews.

**Cellaring** — Simpler versions drink well young, while riper, more concentrated bottlings can develop savoury complexity over several years.

name: Ribolla Gialla
description:
**Ribolla Gialla** is a white grape native to Friuli in north-eastern Italy and the neighbouring Slovenian borderlands, where it is called Rebula. It has a long regional history and has become a favourite for characterful, textured whites.

**In the glass** — In a fresh style it shows citrus, green apple and white-flower aromas with crisp acidity and a stony, mineral edge. It is also a star of skin-contact 'orange' wines, where extended maceration gives amber colour, gentle grip and savoury, nutty depth.

**Where it grows** — Its heartland straddles the Italy–Slovenia border, especially the Collio and Colli Orientali areas, and it is a signature grape of the region's natural and traditional winemakers.

**At the table** — Fresh versions suit seafood and light pasta, while skin-contact styles handle richer, spiced and cured dishes.

**Cellaring** — Crisp examples are best young, but structured and skin-contact wines can age and gain complexity over several years.

name: Trincadeira
description:
**Trincadeira** is a red grape of southern Portugal, closely tied to the warm Alentejo region, where it is a mainstay of the local reds; in the Douro it is often known as Tinta Amarela.

**In the glass** — It produces deeply coloured, medium to full-bodied wines with ripe blackberry and plum fruit, peppery spice and herbal, sometimes floral notes, backed by moderate tannins and decent acidity.

**Where it grows** — It flourishes in the Alentejo's heat, though it is prone to disease in damp conditions and favours dry, sunny sites. It is also used in the Douro and other Portuguese regions, usually as part of a blend.

**At the table** — Its spice and dark fruit pair well with grilled lamb, sausages and hearty stews.

**Cellaring** — Everyday styles are best enjoyed young, while riper, well-made examples can age and gain savoury nuance over the medium term.

name: Müller-Thurgau
description:
**Müller-Thurgau** is a white grape created in 1882 by Hermann Müller, a viticulturist from the Swiss canton of Thurgau, who crossed Riesling with Madeleine Royale — the vine carries both his name and that of his home canton. It became hugely popular for its early ripening and generous yields, spreading fast through German-speaking wine country in the twentieth century.

**In the glass** — light and soft, with gentle aromas of green apple, pear and a faint floral or muscat-like lift; the acidity is modest and the body light, making it easy and approachable rather than intense.

**Where it grows** — long a workhorse of Germany, where it is also called Riesling-Silvaner or Riesling x Sylvaner, and widely planted in Austria, northern Italy (Alto Adige), Switzerland, Hungary and the Czech Republic. Cool sites and lower yields give it more definition and charm.

**At the table** — a friendly match for fresh salads, mild cheeses and light fish dishes.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed young and fresh, within a year or two of the vintage.

name: Furmint
description:
**Furmint** is a white grape most associated with the Tokaj region of Hungary, where it is the backbone of the famous sweet Tokaji Aszú wines made from botrytis-affected grapes. Its naturally high acidity and susceptibility to noble rot make it ideal for both sweet and, increasingly, fine dry wines.

**In the glass** — bright and firm, with orchard fruit, quince, citrus and a smoky, mineral edge; searing acidity gives it energy and a long finish, and it takes well to oak and lees ageing.

**Where it grows** — the star of Tokaj in Hungary, whose vineyards extend across the border into Slovakia; it is also grown in Slovenia, where it is called Šipon, and around Somló in western Hungary. Dry Furmint has become a serious category in its own right.

**At the table** — dry versions suit roast poultry and richer fish; sweet Tokaji pairs beautifully with blue cheese and fruit desserts.

**Cellaring** — excellent ageing potential; the great sweet wines can last for decades, and top dry versions reward several years.

name: Mencía
description:
**Mencía** is a red grape from north-western Spain, at its best in the Bierzo and Ribeira Sacra regions, where it produces fresh, perfumed reds from often steep, slate-strewn hillside vineyards. Known as Jaen in Portugal's Dão, it has enjoyed a real revival as growers seek out old vines and cooler sites.

**In the glass** — medium-bodied and aromatic, with red cherry, raspberry, floral notes and a distinctive mineral, sometimes graphite-like undertone; acidity is lively and tannins are fine, giving an elegant, almost cool feel.

**Where it grows** — centred on Bierzo and Ribeira Sacra in Galicia and Castilla y León, with plantings across Valdeorras and, as Jaen, in Portugal. Old vines on schist and slate deliver the most compelling wines.

**At the table** — versatile with grilled meats, cured pork and mushroom dishes.

**Cellaring** — bright examples drink well young, while structured old-vine bottlings can develop nicely over several years.

name: Welschriesling
description:
**Welschriesling** is a white grape widely grown across Central and Eastern Europe, and despite the name it is entirely unrelated to the true Riesling of Germany. It is a versatile, high-acid variety used for everything from crisp everyday whites to some superb sweet wines.

**In the glass** — typically light and zesty, with green apple, citrus and subtle floral or herbal notes; its hallmark is refreshing acidity, which keeps dry versions lively and gives sweet ones balance.

**Where it grows** — a mainstay across Austria (especially Styria and around the Neusiedlersee), Hungary (as Olaszrizling), Croatia (Graševina), Slovenia, northern Italy, Romania and the Czech Republic. Styles range from simple and dry to concentrated botrytised dessert wines.

**At the table** — the dry style is a natural partner for light appetisers, fried fish and fresh salads.

**Cellaring** — dry versions are best drunk young, though the finest sweet wines can age gracefully.

name: Ugni Blanc
description:
**Ugni Blanc** is a white grape of Italian origin, where it is known as Trebbiano Toscano, and it is one of the most widely planted white varieties in the world. In France it is prized less for table wine than as the base for the distillates of Cognac and Armagnac.

**In the glass** — light, neutral and high in acidity, with delicate lemon and green-apple notes and little aromatic drama; that combination of freshness and restraint is exactly what makes it ideal for distillation.

**Where it grows** — vast plantings in France (the Charente for Cognac, Gascony for Armagnac) and throughout Italy under the Trebbiano name, plus warm regions worldwide. As a table wine it stays crisp and simple; distilled, it becomes the raw material for fine brandy.

**At the table** — the still wine suits simple seafood and light lunchtime fare.

**Cellaring** — meant to be drunk young and fresh.

name: Marquette
description:
**Marquette** is a red hybrid grape developed by the University of Minnesota and released in the 2000s, bred for excellent cold hardiness so that quality red wine could be grown in harsh northern climates. It has become a cornerstone variety for growers in the American Upper Midwest and other cold regions.

**In the glass** — medium-bodied with dark cherry, berry, pepper and often a herbal or spicy note; it keeps good colour and moderate tannin, with lively acidity typical of cold-climate reds.

**Where it grows** — planted across Minnesota, Wisconsin, the northern United States and parts of Canada and Scandinavia, wherever winters are too cold for classic vinifera vines. It handles frost and disease well, making viticulture possible where it otherwise would not be.

**At the table** — good with grilled meats, burgers and hearty comfort food.

**Cellaring** — generally best enjoyed within a few years, though sturdier examples can hold a little longer.

name: Falanghina
description:
**Falanghina** is a white grape from the Campania region of southern Italy, with ancient roots around Naples and the Bay of Naples. It has been a leading light in the revival of Campania's native white varieties and now makes some of the south's most appealing dry whites.

**In the glass** — aromatic and fresh, with citrus, green apple, white flowers and a hint of stone fruit or herbs; bright acidity keeps it crisp, and the body is light to medium with a clean, mineral finish.

**Where it grows** — concentrated in Campania, notably around Benevento (Sannio), the Campi Flegrei and the coast, with scattered plantings elsewhere in southern Italy. Volcanic and coastal soils lend it a saline, mineral character.

**At the table** — a natural with seafood, shellfish and Mediterranean vegetable dishes.

**Cellaring** — best drunk young to catch its freshness, though better examples hold for a few years.

name: Ciliegiolo
description:
**Ciliegiolo** is a red grape from central Italy, long grown in Tuscany, whose name comes from the Italian for cherry, a nod to its signature fruit. Historically a blending partner, it has gained new respect as a characterful variety in its own right, and is closely linked to Sangiovese.

**In the glass** — bright and juicy, with vivid red cherry and berry fruit, floral hints and soft, supple tannins; it is medium-bodied with moderate acidity, giving an easy, perfumed drinkability.
