**Where it grows** — most at home in Tuscany and neighbouring parts of central Italy such as Umbria and Liguria, both blended with Sangiovese and increasingly bottled on its own. Warmer coastal Tuscan sites give it especially ripe, generous fruit.

**At the table** — pairs happily with pasta, cured meats and grilled poultry.

**Cellaring** — mostly made for early, fruit-forward drinking, though some structured versions can age a few years.

name: Verdelho
description:
**Verdelho** is a white grape of Portuguese origin, historically important on the island of Madeira, where it lends its name to one of the classic styles of fortified Madeira wine. It has also found a successful second home as a dry table wine, especially in Australia.

**In the glass** — as a dry wine it is fresh and flavourful, with lime, tropical fruit and a touch of herbs, backed by firm acidity; in fortified Madeira form it is medium-dry, with smoky, nutty, dried-fruit complexity from long cask ageing.

**Where it grows** — native to Portugal and grown on Madeira and the mainland, with notable dry-wine plantings in Australia (the Hunter Valley and beyond). The style shifts sharply from crisp modern white to the age-worthy island fortified wine.

**At the table** — dry Verdelho suits grilled fish and spicy Asian dishes; medium-dry Madeira is lovely with soups or mild cheese.

**Cellaring** — dry versions are best young, while fortified Madeira is famously long-lived.

name: Rabigato
description:
**Rabigato** is a white grape native to the Douro Valley of northern Portugal, where it is one of the traditional varieties used in both white Port and, increasingly, dry Douro whites. It is valued for the freshness and acidity it brings in a warm, dramatic landscape.

**In the glass** — crisp and lively, with citrus, orchard fruit and floral or herbal notes; its high acidity gives white blends structure and a refreshing lift, with a light to medium body.

**Where it grows** — closely tied to the Douro and neighbouring parts of northern Portugal, usually as part of a field blend with other regional white grapes rather than bottled alone. On the schist soils and steep terraces of the Douro it retains welcome acidity despite the heat.

**At the table** — good with grilled fish, shellfish and lighter poultry dishes.

**Cellaring** — generally best enjoyed young for its freshness.

name: Viosinho
description:
**Viosinho** is a white grape from the Douro Valley of northern Portugal, one of the region's prized native varieties for making quality dry white wines and white Port. Though not planted in large quantities, it is highly regarded by growers for the class it brings to a blend.

**In the glass** — aromatic and finely balanced, with citrus, white flowers, stone fruit and a delicate mineral character; it has good body and structure with a fresh finish, giving blends both aroma and weight.

**Where it grows** — centred on the Douro and neighbouring northern Portugal, typically blended with other local whites such as Rabigato and Gouveio, and occasionally bottled on its own. It performs well on the region's schist terraces, holding its poise in a warm climate.

**At the table** — a fine match for roast fish, poultry and creamy sauces.

**Cellaring** — enjoyable young, though the more structured examples can develop over a few years.

name: Malvasia del Chianti
description:
**Malvasia del Chianti** is a white grape from Tuscany in central Italy, one of several distinct varieties that carry the sprawling Malvasia name. It has long been part of the traditional field of grapes grown around the Chianti hills, valued as much for blending and for sweet wine as for standalone bottlings.

**In the glass** — it tends toward a golden hue, with gentle aromas of ripe orchard fruit, honey and dried flowers. On the palate it is soft and rounded, with moderate acidity and a slightly waxy, generous texture rather than sharp definition.

**Where it grows** — its heartland is Tuscany, where it historically joined Trebbiano in white blends and, dried on mats, contributed to the region's amber Vin Santo. Small plantings persist elsewhere in central Italy.

**At the table** — lovely with antipasti, mild cheeses, or (in its sweet form) with almond biscotti for dipping.

**Cellaring** — dry versions are best enjoyed young and fresh, while the sweet Vin Santo style can age gracefully for many years.

name: Fernão Pires
description:
**Fernão Pires** is a white grape widely planted across Portugal, where it is also known as Maria Gomes, particularly around Bairrada. It is one of the country's most versatile and abundant white varieties, appearing in everything from crisp everyday whites to lightly sparkling styles.

**In the glass** — it is markedly aromatic, offering floral, citrus and spicy notes with a hint of terpene lift reminiscent of Muscat. The palate is fresh and fruity, though its naturally lower acidity means the best examples are picked early to keep them lively.

**Where it grows** — it thrives across much of central and western Portugal, including the Tejo and Bairrada regions, adapting to warm conditions and ripening readily.

**At the table** — a natural partner for grilled fish, salads and lighter Portuguese seafood dishes.

**Cellaring** — almost always made to be drunk young, within a year or two, while its aromatics are at their most vivid.

name: Hárslevelű
description:
**Hárslevelű** is a white grape native to Hungary, most closely associated with the famous Tokaj region in the northeast. Its name translates roughly as "linden leaf," and it plays a key supporting role alongside Furmint in the region's celebrated sweet wines.

**In the glass** — it is prized for perfume, showing honeyed, floral and spicy aromas with a distinctive linden-blossom note. The palate is softer and rounder than Furmint, with gentler acidity and a suppler texture.

**Where it grows** — Tokaj is its spiritual home, where it contributes to both dry whites and the luscious botrytised Aszú wines, though it is also grown elsewhere in Hungary.

**At the table** — dry versions suit roast poultry and creamy dishes; sweet styles shine with foie gras or blue cheese.

**Cellaring** — dry wines drink well within a few years, while the sweet Tokaji styles it helps build can age for decades.

name: Trousseau
description:
**Trousseau** is a red grape from the Jura in eastern France, also known as Bastardo, notably in Portugal where it has long featured in fortified wines. In the Jura it makes some of the region's fullest, most structured reds.

**In the glass** — it pours a fairly light but vivid red, with aromas of red berries, cherry, earth and a touch of spice. The palate is more robust than its pale colour suggests, carrying firm acidity and a savoury, slightly rustic grip.

**Where it grows** — the Jura is its classic home, where it is often bottled solo or blended with Poulsard and Pinot Noir. As Bastardo it appears in Portugal, and it is increasingly planted by adventurous growers elsewhere.

**At the table** — pairs beautifully with charcuterie, mushroom dishes and roast poultry.

**Cellaring** — the better examples reward a few years in the cellar, softening and gaining complexity, though many are enjoyable young.

name: Canaiolo
description:
**Canaiolo** is a red grape from Tuscany in central Italy, long grown as the traditional companion to Sangiovese in Chianti. Once a major component of the blend, it now plays a smaller but still valued supporting role.

**In the glass** — it shows a moderate ruby colour with soft aromas of red fruit, plum and dried herbs. On the palate it is gentle and rounded, with lower acidity and softer tannins than Sangiovese, which is precisely why it was used to soften and add flesh to the blend.

**Where it grows** — its home is Tuscany, particularly the Chianti and Chianti Classico zones, with scattered plantings across central Italy. It was also historically dried for use in Vin Santo.

**At the table** — happy alongside pasta with tomato-based sauces, cured meats and roast pork.

**Cellaring** — generally best enjoyed in its youth, offering easy charm rather than long-term ageing potential.

name: Loureiro
description:
**Loureiro** is a white grape from northern Portugal, one of the leading varieties in the Vinho Verde region. Its name nods to the laurel plant, a reference to its distinctly perfumed character.

**In the glass** — it is highly aromatic, with floral, citrus and orchard-fruit notes and that signature hint of laurel or bay. The palate is crisp and light-bodied, driven by bright, refreshing acidity and often a subtle spritz in traditional Vinho Verde.

**Where it grows** — the cool, damp Minho region of northwest Portugal is its heartland, where it is bottled alone or blended with Alvarinho and other local grapes. It is also grown just across the border in Spain's Rías Baixas.

**At the table** — an ideal match for fresh shellfish, grilled sardines and light summer fare.

**Cellaring** — made to be enjoyed young and vibrant, ideally within a year or two of the vintage.

name: Xinomavro
description:
**Xinomavro** is a red grape from northern Greece, most famously grown in Naoussa in Macedonia. Its name means "acid-black," a fitting description for a variety often compared to Nebbiolo for its power and structure. It is widely regarded as one of Greece's finest reds.

**In the glass** — despite a relatively pale, garnet-tinged colour, it delivers intense aromas of red fruit, tomato, olive, dried herbs and a distinctive savoury earthiness. The palate is firmly structured, marked by high acidity and grippy, assertive tannins.

**Where it grows** — Naoussa is its benchmark, with important plantings across northern Greece including Amyndeo and Goumenissa, where cooler sites suit its late ripening.

**At the table** — a natural with lamb, braised meats and tomato-rich Mediterranean dishes.

**Cellaring** — built for the long haul; its acidity and tannin allow the best wines to evolve and improve over a decade or more.

name: Bourboulenc
description:
**Bourboulenc** is a white grape of southern France, one of the permitted varieties in the wines of the Southern Rhône and across the Languedoc. It is usually a blending grape, adding freshness and lift rather than starring on its own.

**In the glass** — it offers delicate aromas of citrus, white flowers and a faintly smoky, herbal note. The palate is light to medium in body, with crisp acidity and a clean, refreshing finish that helps balance richer partners in a blend.

**Where it grows** — it is found throughout the Southern Rhône, including Châteauneuf-du-Pape, and down through the Languedoc, notably in La Clape near the Mediterranean coast where it ripens well.

**At the table** — suits grilled fish, shellfish and Provençal vegetable dishes.

**Cellaring** — generally best drunk young, when its bright acidity and delicate aromatics are at their freshest.

name: Picpoul Noir
description:
**Picpoul Noir** is a red-berried grape of southern France, the dark-skinned counterpart to the better-known white Piquepoul used in Picpoul de Pinet. It is a minor, traditional variety, permitted as a blending component in parts of the Southern Rhône.

**In the glass** — it tends to produce pale, lightly coloured reds with modest tannin and fresh, red-fruited aromas. Its most notable trait, echoed in its name, is a lively, tangy acidity.

**Where it grows** — it is a historic variety of the Rhône and wider Mediterranean south of France, though plantings today are small and it is rarely bottled on its own.

**At the table** — its freshness suits lighter fare such as charcuterie and simple grilled dishes.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed young, as a fresh and easygoing wine rather than one for the cellar.

name: Saperavi
description:
**Saperavi** is a red grape from Georgia, the ancient winemaking country in the Caucasus, with its stronghold in the eastern region of Kakheti. Its name means "dye" or "paint," and it is one of the rare teinturier grapes whose flesh is red as well as its skin.

**In the glass** — it delivers a deep, inky, near-opaque colour with dark aromas of black fruit, plum and spice. The palate is full-bodied and powerful, combining high acidity with substantial tannin, giving a wine of real intensity and grip.

**Where it grows** — Kakheti is its heartland, where it is made both in modern styles and in the traditional qvevri clay vessels buried underground. It is also grown in neighbouring countries and increasingly further afield.

**At the table** — a hearty companion to grilled and roast meats, stews and rich Georgian cuisine.

**Cellaring** — its structure and acidity make it a strong candidate for ageing, developing complexity over many years.

name: Grillo
description:
**Grillo** is a white grape from Sicily in southern Italy, historically prized as a key component of the island's fortified Marsala wine. In recent decades it has been reinvented as a source of characterful dry table whites.

**In the glass** — it shows aromas of citrus, ripe stone fruit and a subtle herbal or floral edge. The palate is medium-bodied and refreshing, holding good acidity that keeps it lively despite Sicily's warm climate.

**Where it grows** — western Sicily around Marsala is its home, where it thrives in the heat and retains freshness; it is now planted across the island for varietal whites as well as its traditional fortified role.

**At the table** — excellent with grilled fish, seafood pasta and Mediterranean vegetable dishes.

**Cellaring** — most dry versions are best enjoyed within a couple of years, though some fuller, richer examples can hold a little longer.

name: Malvasia Istriana
description:
**Malvasia Istriana** is a white grape from the Istrian peninsula, straddling the border of north-eastern Italy (Friuli) and Croatia. It is one of the many distinct varieties that carry the "Malvasia" name, and it is prized locally as a characterful dry white rather than the sweet wines the family is often known for.

**In the glass** — expect a pale straw wine with gentle aromas of white flowers, ripe apple, almond and a faint saline or herbal note. On the palate it is dry and medium-bodied, with softer acidity and a subtly bitter, nutty finish.

**Where it grows** — its heartland is Friuli-Venezia Giulia and the Istrian coast of Slovenia and Croatia, where the maritime climate suits it. Styles range from crisp, fresh bottlings to richer, skin-contact and oak-aged versions made by ambitious producers.

**At the table** — a natural match for seafood, prosciutto and lightly dressed vegetable dishes.

**Cellaring** — usually best enjoyed within a few years, though structured, skin-contact examples can develop with modest cellaring.

name: Insolia
description:
**Insolia** is a white grape native to Sicily, where it is also widely spelled Inzolia. It has long been a workhorse of the island, used both for dry table wines and historically as a component in fortified Marsala.

**In the glass** — the wines are typically pale straw, offering aromas of ripe pear, citrus, almond and a whisper of dried herbs. The palate is soft and medium-bodied with moderate acidity and a characteristic gently nutty, slightly bitter finish.

**Where it grows** — Sicily is its home, particularly the warmer western reaches around Marsala and the central hills, and it also appears in Tuscany under the name Ansonica. Cooler sites and careful winemaking yield fresher, more aromatic styles, while warmer zones give rounder, fuller wines.

**At the table** — pairs happily with grilled fish, shellfish and Mediterranean vegetable dishes.

**Cellaring** — designed for early drinking; enjoy it young while its freshness is at its peak.

name: Concord
description:
**Concord** is a dark-skinned American grape derived from the native species Vitis labrusca, developed in Massachusetts in the mid-19th century. Hugely important in the United States, it is the classic grape behind grape juice, jelly and kosher sweet wines as much as it is a wine grape.

**In the glass** — it is unmistakable, with a deep purple colour and the intense "foxy", grapey aroma typical of labrusca, alongside notes of jam and candied fruit. Wines are usually made in a sweet or off-dry style to balance high natural acidity, and tannins are light.

**Where it grows** — it thrives across the eastern and midwestern United States, notably New York, and tolerates cold winters far better than European vinifera vines.

**At the table** — the sweeter styles suit desserts, or simply casual sipping.

**Cellaring** — not built for the cellar; drink it young and fresh.

name: Chancellor
description:
**Chancellor** is a red French-American hybrid grape, bred in France and later planted widely in the cooler wine regions of North America. It was created to combine disease resistance and cold tolerance with a cleaner, more European flavour profile than the native labrusca grapes.

**In the glass** — it gives deeply coloured, medium-bodied red wines with dark-fruit aromas, a savoury edge and moderate tannins, generally free of the strong "foxy" character found in many hybrids.

**Where it grows** — today it is most associated with the eastern United States and Canada, where its hardiness suits challenging climates, though it originated in France among the classic French hybrid crossings bred for wine.

**At the table** — a versatile partner for roasted meats, stews and hearty everyday fare.

**Cellaring** — most examples are best enjoyed within a few years, though better-structured wines can hold for a while.

name: Petit Manseng
description:
**Petit Manseng** is a white grape from the foothills of the French Pyrenees, most famous in the Jurançon appellation of south-west France. With its small, thick-skinned berries, it is celebrated above all for luscious sweet wines made from grapes left to shrivel on the vine.

**In the glass** — it combines remarkable intensity with searing acidity, offering aromas of candied citrus, pineapple, apricot, honey and exotic spice. Even when made dry, it keeps a vivid freshness and concentrated tropical character.

**Where it grows** — its heartland is Jurançon and the wider south-west of France, but it has found notable success in warmer New World regions such as Virginia in the United States.

**At the table** — sweet versions shine with blue cheese and fruit desserts; dry styles suit rich fish and poultry.

**Cellaring** — the sweet wines have excellent ageing potential, developing complexity over many years thanks to their high acidity.

name: Scheurebe
description:
**Scheurebe** is an aromatic white grape bred in Germany in the early 20th century, the work of viticulturist Georg Scheu, whose name it carries. A crossing that involves Riesling, it was designed to deliver ripeness and perfume, and it excels across dry, off-dry and sweet styles.

**In the glass** — it is intensely aromatic, with striking notes of pink grapefruit, blackcurrant leaf, ripe peach and honeyed exotic fruit. The palate is racy and full of flavour, backed by lively acidity that keeps even sweeter wines balanced.

**Where it grows** — Germany, especially the Pfalz and Rheinhessen, is its home, and it is also grown in Austria (where it is sometimes called Sämling 88).

**At the table** — dry versions pair with spicy Asian dishes; sweet ones with fruit tarts and rich cheeses.

**Cellaring** — the sweet, high-acid examples age gracefully; dry styles are best enjoyed within a few years.

name: Arneis
description:
**Arneis** is a white grape from Piedmont in north-west Italy, most closely tied to the Roero hills across the river from the Barolo zone. Once nearly forgotten, it was revived in the late 20th century and is now a benchmark northern Italian white.

**In the glass** — it offers a pale gold colour with delicate aromas of pear, white peach, almond and chamomile. The palate is dry and medium-bodied, with a rounded texture, relatively soft acidity and a gently bitter, nutty finish.

**Where it grows** — Roero and the Langhe in Piedmont are its heartland, where it appears in the Roero Arneis and Langhe Arneis appellations; small plantings exist elsewhere, including Australia and the United States.

**At the table** — a fine match for antipasti, risotto and delicate fish dishes.

**Cellaring** — generally best enjoyed young and fresh, within two or three years of the vintage.

name: Muscardin
description:
**Muscardin** is a red grape from the southern Rhône Valley in France, best known as one of the many permitted varieties in the Châteauneuf-du-Pape blend. It is a minor, relatively rare grape, almost always used in small proportions rather than on its own.

**In the glass** — it typically contributes lighter colour, fresh acidity and a floral, red-fruited lift to a blend, adding perfume and finesse rather than weight or deep tannin.

**Where it grows** — it is found almost exclusively in the southern Rhône around Châteauneuf-du-Pape, where a handful of growers keep it as part of the traditional field of authorised varieties.

**At the table** — as part of a Rhône blend, it suits roasted and grilled meats and Provençal herb-scented dishes.

**Cellaring** — its ageing role follows the blend it belongs to; on its own it is a supporting, freshness-lending variety rather than a keeper.

name: Vaccarèse
description:
**Vaccarèse** is a red grape of the southern Rhône Valley in France, counted among the traditional varieties permitted in Châteauneuf-du-Pape. Also known locally as Brun Argenté, it is a rare grape used almost entirely in small blending amounts.

**In the glass** — it tends to give lightly coloured, fresh wine with modest tannin, bright acidity and a peppery, herbal, red-fruited character that adds lift and savour to a blend.

**Where it grows** — its home is the southern Rhône around Châteauneuf-du-Pape, where only a few producers still cultivate it as part of the appellation's classic mix of grapes.

**At the table** — within a Rhône blend it complements grilled lamb, game and herb-driven Mediterranean cooking.

**Cellaring** — a minor blending component rather than a stand-alone wine; its longevity depends on the blend it joins.

name: Terret Noir
description:
**Terret Noir** is a red grape from the Languedoc in southern France, and one of the old traditional varieties permitted in Châteauneuf-du-Pape. It belongs to the wider Terret family, which unusually includes black, grey and white-berried forms on closely related vines.

**In the glass** — it is valued for freshness, giving lightly coloured, relatively pale reds with brisk acidity, light tannin and a peppery, herbal edge that lends nerve to a blend.

**Where it grows** — its base is the Languedoc, and it also appears in small amounts in the southern Rhône, where it plays a supporting role in Châteauneuf-du-Pape rather than a starring one.

**At the table** — as a blend component it suits grilled meats and rustic Mediterranean dishes.

**Cellaring** — prized for its refreshing quality rather than power; generally not a variety made for long ageing on its own.

name: Fiano
description:
**Fiano** is a white grape from Campania in southern Italy, with a heritage stretching back to antiquity around the town of Avellino. It is one of the south's most respected white varieties, capable of wines with real depth and character.

**In the glass** — it shows a golden hue and complex aromas of honey, hazelnut, ripe pear, dried herbs and a distinctive smoky, waxy note. The palate is dry and medium- to full-bodied, with a firm structure, good acidity and a long, savoury finish.

**Where it grows** — its benchmark is Fiano di Avellino in Campania, and it is also widely planted across Sicily and Puglia, as well as farther afield in Australia, where it suits warm climates well.

**At the table** — excellent with grilled fish, shellfish, poultry and creamy pasta.

**Cellaring** — unusually age-worthy for a southern Italian white, the best examples gain nutty complexity over several years.

name: Assyrtiko
description:
**Assyrtiko** is a white grape that hails from the Greek island of Santorini, where it grows in volcanic ash and pumice, and it has become the flag-bearer for Greek fine wine on the world stage.

**In the glass** — expect a pale, bright wine with sharp citrus, lemon pith and a striking mineral, almost salty edge; the palate is bone-dry with racy acidity and a lean, taut body that keeps its nerve even in hot vintages.

**Where it grows** — Santorini remains the benchmark, where old vines are coiled into basket shapes to shelter from the wind, but it now thrives across mainland Greece and has spread to Australia and beyond, where warmer sites tend to soften its edges and add riper stone-fruit notes.

**At the table** — a natural partner for grilled fish, fried calamari and other seafood.

**Cellaring** — one of the few dry whites of the Mediterranean built to age, developing waxy, honeyed depth over five to ten years or more.

name: Dornfelder
description:
**Dornfelder** is a red grape bred in Germany in 1955, a deliberate crossing designed to give the country's cool vineyards a variety with deep colour and reliable ripeness.

**In the glass** — it is prized precisely for its inky, dark-purple hue, offering juicy black cherry and blackberry fruit, soft tannins, medium body and gentle acidity that make it approachable and easy to drink.

**Where it grows** — Germany is its heartland, particularly the Pfalz and Rheinhessen regions, where it ranges from simple fruity quaffers to more ambitious oak-aged bottlings; small plantings exist in England and elsewhere in northern Europe.

**At the table** — happy alongside roast pork, sausages and hearty weeknight fare.

**Cellaring** — most versions are made for early, cheerful drinking, though the more structured, barrel-aged examples can hold for several years.

name: Bobal
description:
**Bobal** is a red grape native to eastern Spain, closely tied to the Utiel-Requena region inland from Valencia, where it has long been a workhorse of bulk production but is increasingly taken seriously.

**In the glass** — it gives a deeply coloured wine with dark berry and plum fruit, notable freshness thanks to naturally high acidity, and firm, sometimes rustic tannins that reward careful winemaking.

**Where it grows** — its stronghold is the high, continental plateau of Utiel-Requena and neighbouring areas of the Valencian and Castilla-La Mancha interior, where old bush vines yield concentrated fruit; historically much went into blends and rosé.

**At the table** — pairs well with grilled lamb, chorizo and robust stews.

**Cellaring** — everyday bottlings drink best young and fresh, while old-vine, more serious cuvées can develop over a handful of years.

name: Turbiana
description:
**Turbiana** is a white grape from northern Italy, grown chiefly around Lake Garda in the Lugana zone straddling Lombardy and the Veneto, and long confusingly labelled Trebbiano di Lugana despite being genetically distinct.

**In the glass** — it offers a delicate, medium-bodied wine with white flowers, almond, citrus and green-apple notes, fresh acidity and a subtle savoury, sometimes faintly bitter finish.

**Where it grows** — its home is the clay-rich soils of Lugana on the southern shore of Lake Garda, where it produces both crisp, early-drinking styles and richer, more textured wines that can see time on lees or in barrel.

**At the table** — lovely with lake fish, risotto and lighter poultry.

**Cellaring** — most is enjoyed young, but the better single-estate versions can gain complexity over several years.

name: De Chaunac
description:
**De Chaunac** is a red hybrid of mixed European and American parentage, developed in France and later valued across cooler parts of North America for its disease resistance and tolerance of hard winters.

**In the glass** — it produces a fairly deeply coloured red with tart dark-berry fruit, moderate to high acidity, light-to-medium body and generally soft tannins.

**Where it grows** — it found its footing in cooler winegrowing areas of eastern Canada and the northeastern United States, where its resistance to frost made it valuable, though plantings have declined as growers shifted to other varieties.

**At the table** — suits simple roast meats and casual, everyday dishes.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed young while its fruit is fresh.

name: Frontenac
description:
**Frontenac** is a red hybrid grape developed by the University of Minnesota's breeding programme, created to survive brutally cold winters while still ripening a usable crop.

**In the glass** — it is known for very deep colour and bracing acidity, with cherry and dark-berry flavours and often a plummy, sometimes jammy character; tannins are typically modest.

**Where it grows** — it is a mainstay of the upper Midwest of the United States and other cold-climate regions of North America, where it is vinified as dry red, rosé and port-style sweet wine to tame its natural sharpness.

**At the table** — the sweeter styles flatter chocolate, while dry versions handle grilled and smoked meats.

**Cellaring** — generally made for early drinking, though fortified and sweet examples keep longer.

name: Grenache Gris
description:
**Grenache Gris** is a pale-berried mutation of the widely planted Grenache, generally grouped with the white varieties and long associated with southern France and northern Spain.

**In the glass** — it yields a fuller, textural white with a subtle pink-grey tint in the fruit, showing ripe orchard fruit, citrus peel, a gently nutty or saline note, soft acidity and appealing weight on the palate.

**Where it grows** — old vines survive in Roussillon in the French Mediterranean and across the border in Catalonia, where they contribute richness to dry whites and to the region's traditional fortified wines; interest in reviving these old parcels has grown.

**At the table** — good with grilled vegetables, roast chicken and richer seafood.

**Cellaring** — everyday styles drink young, but old-vine and oxidative examples can age gracefully.

name: Friulano
description:
**Friulano** is a white grape most closely identified with the Friuli region of northeastern Italy, where it long went by the name Tocai Friulano before European labelling rules forced a change; it is the same variety known elsewhere as Sauvignonasse.

**In the glass** — it is a dry, medium-bodied white with pear, almond and fresh-herb aromas, a gently savoury character and a signature bitter-almond twist on the finish, balanced by moderate acidity.

**Where it grows** — Friuli, especially the Collio and Colli Orientali hills, is its spiritual home, producing crisp, food-friendly whites; it is also grown across the border in Slovenia and, historically, in parts of the Americas.

**At the table** — a classic match for prosciutto and cured meats.

**Cellaring** — usually best in its first few years, though top examples can hold.

name: Colombard
description:
**Colombard** is a white grape from the Charente region of western France, historically grown as a base for the distillation of Cognac and Armagnac thanks to its naturally high acidity and modest alcohol.

**In the glass** — as a table wine it is light, crisp and refreshing, with green apple, citrus and sometimes a subtle floral or grassy lift, high acidity and a lean, easy body.

**Where it grows** — beyond its brandy heartland in southwest France it is widely planted in the Côtes de Gascogne for zippy everyday whites, and it became especially important in South Africa and California as a productive, dependable variety.

**At the table** — an obliging apéritif and a friend to salads and light seafood.

**Cellaring** — made to be drunk young and fresh.

name: Gros Manseng
description:
**Gros Manseng** is a white grape from the foothills of the French Pyrenees, particularly the Jurançon area in the southwest, where it plays a leading role in both dry and sweet wines.

**In the glass** — it delivers a lively, aromatic white with grapefruit, passion fruit, stone fruit and a distinctive exotic edge, carried by brisk, mouth-watering acidity and good body; with larger berries and higher yields than its relative Petit Manseng, it is the more productive of the two.

**Where it grows** — it is centred on Jurançon and the wider Gascony region, where it makes crisp dry whites and, when late-harvested, richly fruity off-dry to sweet styles that retain freshness.

**At the table** — the dry style suits spicy dishes; the sweet style loves blue cheese and foie gras.

**Cellaring** — dry wines drink young, while the sweet versions can age well.

name: Bosco
description:
**Bosco** is a white grape from the Italian region of Liguria, above all the steep coastal terraces of the Cinque Terre, where it anchors the local wines clinging to the cliffs above the sea.

**In the glass** — it makes a fresh, medium-bodied white with citrus, herbal and delicately saline notes, moderate acidity and a subtle Mediterranean character shaped by its seaside home.

**Where it grows** — it is grown almost exclusively along the Ligurian coast, forming the backbone of Cinque Terre whites and, most famously, the rare and prized sweet Sciacchetrà made from dried grapes.

**At the table** — a natural with anchovies, pesto and the region's seafood; the sweet Sciacchetrà suits dessert or cheese.

**Cellaring** — dry wines are best young, while Sciacchetrà can age for many years.

name: Albarola
description:
**Albarola** is a white grape from the Ligurian coast of northwest Italy, best known as a supporting player in the seaside blends of the Cinque Terre. It rarely stars on its own, but it lends freshness and structure to some of Italy's most dramatic terraced vineyards.

**In the glass** — pale straw in colour, with a fairly restrained, neutral nose of green apple, citrus and a faint saline note. The palate is light-bodied, crisp and brisk with acidity, finishing clean rather than aromatic.

**Where it grows** — its home is Liguria, especially around the Cinque Terre and the wider Riviera, where it is blended with Bosco and Vermentino. Plantings are modest and largely confined to this stretch of coast.

**At the table** — a natural match for anchovies, fried seafood and other simple dishes of the Ligurian shore.

**Cellaring** — made to be drunk young and fresh, ideally within a year or two of the vintage.

name: Agiorgitiko
description:
**Agiorgitiko** is a red grape from Greece and one of the country's most widely planted and versatile varieties, with its spiritual home in Nemea in the northeastern Peloponnese. Sometimes called Saint George, it can turn its hand to almost any style, from fresh rosé to deep, oak-aged reds.

**In the glass** — a deep ruby colour with generous aromas of ripe red and black fruit, plum and soft spice. The palate is supple and fleshy, with moderate acidity and smooth, rounded tannins that make it approachable.

**Where it grows** — Nemea is the classic region, where higher-altitude vineyards give more structured wines, while lower sites yield softer, fruitier ones. It is planted widely across mainland Greece and often blended with international varieties.

**At the table** — pairs happily with lamb, grilled meats and tomato-based Mediterranean dishes.

**Cellaring** — everyday versions drink well young, while the best barrel-aged Nemea reds can develop over several years.

name: Nero di Troia
description:
**Nero di Troia** is a red grape from Puglia in southern Italy, also known as Uva di Troia, and one of the region's three signature native reds alongside Primitivo and Negroamaro. It ripens late and is prized for the firmness and structure it brings.

**In the glass** — deep ruby to garnet, with aromas of dark cherry, blackberry, dried herbs and a peppery, slightly floral edge. The palate is full and firmly tannic, with fresh acidity that keeps it lively.

**Where it grows** — its heartland is northern Puglia, particularly around Castel del Monte, and it also features in the wines of Cerignola. It is very much a regional specialty, little seen elsewhere.

**At the table** — good with roast lamb, braised beef and hard sheep's-milk cheeses.

**Cellaring** — its tannin and acidity give it real ageing potential, with the more serious bottlings softening and gaining complexity over several years.

name: Croatina
description:
**Croatina** is a red grape from northern Italy, most at home in the hills of Oltrepò Pavese in Lombardy and the neighbouring Colli Piacentini in Emilia. It is often confusingly labelled Bonarda locally, though it is a distinct variety.

**In the glass** — deeply coloured, with aromas of blackberry, dark plum and a wild, slightly earthy character. The palate tends to be full and tannic with lively acidity, and it is frequently made in a lightly sparkling, frizzante style that softens its grip.

**Where it grows** — Oltrepò Pavese and Colli Piacentini are its strongholds, where it appears both on its own and as a key part of the Gutturnio blend with Barbera. Plantings are concentrated in this corner of northern Italy.

**At the table** — a good foil for salami, cured meats and rich pasta.

**Cellaring** — usually enjoyed young and fresh, especially in its frizzante form, though firmer still versions can hold for a few years.

name: Verdejo
description:
**Verdejo** is a white grape from central Spain and the defining variety of the Rueda region, where it produces bright, aromatic wines that helped modernise Spanish white wine. It has become one of the country's most popular and recognisable whites.

**In the glass** — pale with green tints, offering aromas of citrus, green apple, fennel and fresh herbs, often with a distinctive bitter-almond twist. The palate is crisp and textured, with good acidity and a characteristic gently bitter finish.

**Where it grows** — Rueda, on the high plains of Castilla y León, is its home, where old vines and cool nights preserve its freshness. It is occasionally blended with Sauvignon Blanc or Viura.

**At the table** — excellent with grilled fish, seafood, salads and fresh goat's cheese.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed young and vibrant, though some oak-aged or lees-aged examples can develop pleasingly over a few years.

name: Garganega
description:
**Garganega** is a white grape from the Veneto in northeast Italy and the backbone of Soave, one of Italy's classic white wines. An ancient variety, it can range from simple and easygoing to remarkably refined.

**In the glass** — pale straw to gold, with delicate aromas of white flowers, ripe pear, citrus and a signature note of bitter almond. The palate is medium-bodied with fresh acidity and a subtle, savoury texture that gains depth from good sites.

**Where it grows** — Soave and Gambellara are its heartland, where volcanic soils and hillside vineyards give the finest, most mineral wines. It is also used, semi-dried, for sweet Recioto di Soave.

**At the table** — pairs well with risotto, white fish, poultry and fresh cheeses.

**Cellaring** — everyday versions drink young, but top single-vineyard Soave can age gracefully for a decade, deepening into honeyed, nutty complexity.

name: Lagrein
description:
**Lagrein** is a red grape native to the far north of Italy, thriving in the alpine valleys of Alto Adige around Bolzano. A relative of Teroldego, it makes darkly coloured, characterful reds that stand apart from the region's lighter styles.

**In the glass** — inky, deep purple, with aromas of blackberry, dark plum, violet and a note of cocoa or bitter chocolate. The palate is full-bodied and richly fruited, with firm tannins balanced by refreshing acidity and a faintly bitter finish.

**Where it grows** — Alto Adige is its home, particularly the warmer valley floors near Bolzano, and it is also planted in small amounts in nearby Trentino. It is a regional specialty rarely found beyond this alpine corner.

**At the table** — a fine match for venison, braised beef, grilled sausages and mountain cheeses.

**Cellaring** — approachable young, the more structured bottlings reward several years in the cellar.

name: Oseleta
description:
**Oseleta** is a red grape from the Veneto in northeast Italy, a nearly forgotten variety that was rescued from near-extinction in recent decades. It is prized as a blending grape that adds colour, tannin and backbone.

**In the glass** — very deeply coloured, with concentrated aromas of dark berries, spice and a herbal edge. Its small, thick-skinned berries give wines that are firmly tannic and structured, which is why it usually plays a supporting rather than a solo role.

**Where it grows** — the Valpolicella zone of the Veneto is its home, where it is added in small proportions to Valpolicella and Amarone blends to reinforce structure. Plantings remain very limited.

**At the table** — best alongside the rich meats and braises that suit the Veneto's fuller reds.

**Cellaring** — its tannin and depth make it well suited to ageing, particularly within the long-lived blends it contributes to.

name: Bical
description:
**Bical** is a white grape from Portugal, most associated with the Bairrada region on the Atlantic coast. It is valued for its natural acidity, which makes it useful for both still whites and traditional-method sparkling wines.

**In the glass** — pale and bright, with aromas of citrus, apple and a light floral, sometimes peachy character. The palate is fresh and crisp, driven by high acidity that keeps the wine lively.

**Where it grows** — Bairrada is its heartland, where the cool, damp maritime climate suits its brisk style, and it also appears in the neighbouring Dão. It is largely a Portuguese regional variety.

**At the table** — good with seafood, grilled fish and the region's roast suckling pig.

**Cellaring** — usually enjoyed young, though its firm acidity means the best examples, especially sparkling ones, can age well.

name: Cerceal
description:
**Cerceal** is a white grape used in central Portugal, where the name is associated with the Dão and Bairrada regions. It is grown chiefly for the freshness and acidity it brings to blends.

**In the glass** — pale in colour, with a restrained nose of citrus, green apple and subtle herbal notes. The palate is crisp and refreshing, marked above all by lively acidity.

**Where it grows** — it is found in the Dão and Bairrada areas of Portugal, generally as a component in white blends rather than a solo variety. Plantings are modest and regional.

**At the table** — a natural partner for fish, shellfish and lighter poultry dishes.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed young while its fresh acidity is at its most vibrant.

name: Trajadura
description:
**Trajadura** is a white grape from northern Portugal, where it is one of the varieties behind Vinho Verde. Known as Treixadura across the border in Galicia, it is valued for adding body and gentle fruit to blends.

**In the glass** — pale straw, with mild aromas of apple, pear and citrus and a soft floral touch. The palate is relatively low in acidity and rounder than many of its blending partners, lending weight and texture rather than sharpness.

**Where it grows** — the Minho region of northwest Portugal is its home, where it is blended with the more aromatic Loureiro and Alvarinho in Vinho Verde. It is also important just over the border in Galicia's Ribeiro.

**At the table** — pairs well with grilled fish, seafood and lighter salads.

**Cellaring** — made to be drunk young and fresh, within a year or two of the vintage.

name: Pedro Ximénez
description:
**Pedro Ximénez** is a white grape from southern Spain, most closely tied to Montilla-Moriles and Jerez, where it is prized for making some of the darkest, sweetest fortified wines in the world.

**In the glass** — Sun-dried on mats before pressing to concentrate its sugars, it turns into an almost black, syrupy nectar bursting with raisin, fig, molasses, dates and espresso, low in acidity and intensely, richly sweet.

**Where it grows** — Its heartland is Andalucía, above all Montilla-Moriles, though it also appears in Jerez as a sweetening component for sherry. Small plantings exist in Australia and parts of Latin America. In cooler spots or when picked fresh it can yield a lighter dry wine, but its calling remains sweet.

**At the table** — Pour it over vanilla ice cream, or match it with blue cheese, dark chocolate or a walnut tart.

**Cellaring** — The sweet, high-sugar styles are near-immortal, holding and deepening for decades in bottle.

name: Nerello Cappuccio
description:
**Nerello Cappuccio** is a red grape from Sicily, grown chiefly on the volcanic slopes of Mount Etna, where it plays a supporting role alongside the more celebrated Nerello Mascalese.

**In the glass** — It tends to give softer, rounder wines with a deep, almost inky colour, ripe red-berry fruit and gentle, supple tannins, adding flesh and colour where its partner brings structure and perfume.

**Where it grows** — Almost all of it is planted on Etna, where it is usually blended into Etna Rosso rather than bottled alone. A little is found elsewhere in Sicily, but its identity is bound to the mountain's dark volcanic soils.

**At the table** — Good with grilled lamb, roasted vegetables or a tomato-rich pasta.

**Cellaring** — Drinkable young for its fruit, though in serious Etna blends it can age gracefully over several years.

name: Malvasía
description:
**Malvasía** is a white grape — or more accurately a sprawling family of loosely related varieties — long grown around the Mediterranean, from Spain and Portugal to Italy and the Greek islands from which the name is thought to derive.

**In the glass** — Styles range widely, but many share an aromatic, floral character with notes of apricot, peach, honey and a whiff of musk, typically with moderate acidity and a soft, generous texture.

**Where it grows** — Because it is a family rather than a single grape, its members turn up across Iberia, Italy, the Canary Islands, Madeira and beyond, made as dry whites, aromatic blends and rich sweet or fortified wines.

**At the table** — Dry versions suit seafood and lighter poultry; sweet ones pair with fruit tarts and soft cheeses.

**Cellaring** — Most dry styles are best enjoyed young, while the sweet and fortified expressions can age remarkably well.

name: Bacchus
description:
**Bacchus** is a white grape bred in Germany in the twentieth century, a crossing designed to ripen reliably in cool climates while keeping plenty of aromatic character.

**In the glass** — It is prized for its perfume, showing elderflower, grapefruit, gooseberry and green herbs, with a soft, gently floral palate and relatively modest acidity when fully ripe.

**Where it grows** — Long a workhorse in Germany's cooler regions, it has found a notable second home in England, where its ability to ripen in marginal conditions makes it a signature aromatic white. It is usually made dry to off-dry and unoaked.

**At the table** — Lovely with fresh goat cheese, salads, or delicate white fish.

**Cellaring** — Made to be drunk young and fresh, ideally within a couple of years of the vintage.

name: Airén
description:
**Airén** is a white grape native to central Spain, above all the vast plains of La Mancha, and it has historically been one of the most widely planted varieties in the country by area.

**In the glass** — It typically gives a pale, light-bodied wine with a neutral, subtly fruity character, gentle citrus and apple notes and soft acidity, making it easy and unassuming rather than dramatic.

**Where it grows** — Its heartland is the hot, dry expanse of La Mancha and surrounding central Spain, where its drought resistance suits the harsh climate. Much of the crop goes to distillation for brandy or into inexpensive everyday whites, though careful modern winemaking can produce fresher, cleaner styles.

**At the table** — A simple partner for tapas, fried fish or light snacks.

**Cellaring** — Best enjoyed young while it is fresh and crisp.

name: Grolleau
description:
**Grolleau** is a red grape from France's Loire Valley, traditionally valued for its productivity and its role in the region's rosés rather than for making bold, structured reds.

**In the glass** — It produces light, fresh wines with bright red-fruit flavours, high acidity and low tannin; as a rosé it is delicate and easy-drinking, with crisp berry and floral notes.

**Where it grows** — It is grown mainly in Anjou and Touraine, where it is a backbone of Rosé d'Anjou and other Loire pink wines. Once very widely planted, it has given ground to more prestigious varieties but remains characterful in the right hands.

**At the table** — Serve it chilled with charcuterie, summer salads or a picnic spread.

**Cellaring** — Made to be drunk young and fresh; it holds little benefit from ageing.

name: Picardan
description:
**Picardan** is a white grape from the southern Rhône in France, best known as one of the many permitted varieties in the blend of Châteauneuf-du-Pape.

**In the glass** — It is a fairly neutral, gently aromatic grape, typically contributing freshness and a light, subtle character rather than pronounced flavour, with modest intensity and moderate acidity.

**Where it grows** — Its plantings are small and concentrated in the southern Rhône, where it survives largely thanks to its place among the grapes historically allowed in Châteauneuf-du-Pape. It is almost always a minor blending component rather than a wine made on its own.

**At the table** — Suited to light Mediterranean dishes, herbed vegetables and simple fish.

**Cellaring** — Generally best enjoyed young for its freshness.

name: Palomino
description:
**Palomino** is a white grape from Andalucía in southern Spain, the foundation of dry sherry and the classic base variety of the vineyards around Jerez. It is also known as Listán Blanco.

**In the glass** — As a still wine it is fairly neutral, low in acidity and light in fruit, but under the sherry-making process it transforms — fino and manzanilla gain a bracing, salty, yeasty tang from flor, while oloroso styles turn rich, nutty and savoury.

**Where it grows** — Its home is the chalky albariza soils of the Jerez region, and as Listán Blanco it is important in the Canary Islands, where it makes distinctive dry table whites.

**At the table** — Dry sherry is superb with olives, almonds, jamón and seafood.

**Cellaring** — Fino styles are best fresh, while oloroso and aged sherries can last for decades.

name: Moscatel Roxo
description:
**Moscatel Roxo** is a pink-skinned member of the Muscat family, grown in Portugal and associated above all with the Setúbal peninsula south of Lisbon.

**In the glass** — Like other Muscats it is intensely aromatic, offering orange blossom, rose, ripe grape and honeyed spice, but as a fortified wine it takes on a warm, deep character with raisin, dried apricot and marmalade notes over a rich, sweet palate.

**Where it grows** — It is a specialty of Setúbal, where it is comparatively rare and often bottled as a prized fortified Moscatel, quite distinct from the more common white Moscatel of the same region.

**At the table** — Delicious with almond desserts, dried fruit or a wedge of aged cheese.

**Cellaring** — The fortified sweet style ages beautifully, gaining complexity over many years in bottle.

name: País
description:
**País** is a red grape long established in Chile, where it was among the first varieties planted by early settlers; it is the same grape known elsewhere as Listán Prieto.

**In the glass** — It usually gives a pale, light-bodied red with bright, tart red-fruit flavours, fresh acidity and soft tannins, rustic and juicy in a thirst-quenching way rather than deep or powerful.

**Where it grows** — Its stronghold is southern Chile, especially areas like Maule and Itata, where old, dry-farmed bush vines have won new appreciation from winemakers seeking authenticity and lighter styles. The same variety appears as Mission in North America.

**At the table** — A friendly match for grilled meats, empanadas and casual, spicy fare.

**Cellaring** — Best enjoyed young and fresh, though old-vine bottlings can show surprising depth.

name: Poulsard
description:
**Poulsard** is a red grape from the Jura in eastern France, a regional specialty famous for producing wines so pale they can look almost like rosés.

**In the glass** — It is thin-skinned and low in pigment, giving delicate, translucent reds with high-toned red-fruit and floral aromas, bright acidity and very light tannins; charming and ethereal rather than robust.

**Where it grows** — It is grown almost entirely in the Jura, where it is a signature of the region's light reds and often blended with Trousseau and Pinot Noir. Its low colour and fragility make it a niche, characterful variety unlikely to spread far beyond home.

**At the table** — Serve lightly chilled with poultry, charcuterie or mushroom dishes.

**Cellaring** — Approachable young, though good examples can develop intriguing complexity with a few years in bottle.

name: Prokupac
description:
**Prokupac** is a red grape variety native to Serbia, where it has long been regarded as the backbone of the country's traditional reds and a symbol of local winemaking heritage.

**In the glass** — It gives a medium-bodied wine of bright ruby colour, with red-fruit and sour-cherry aromas, a touch of dried herbs, brisk acidity and moderate, gently grippy tannins.

**Where it grows** — Its heartland is southern and central Serbia, particularly around the Župa and Toplica areas, where it appears both as a lighter rosé and as a more structured, oak-aged red as growers have worked to elevate its reputation.

**At the table** — Lovely with grilled meats, paprika-spiced stews and rustic charcuterie.

**Cellaring** — Most examples are made to drink within a few years, though the more ambitious, barrel-aged bottlings can develop pleasantly over the medium term.

name: Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso
description:
**Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso** is a red grape from the Friuli region of northeastern Italy, its name a nod to the red stalk ("peduncolo rosso") that distinguishes it within the wider Refosco family.

**In the glass** — It produces a deeply coloured, medium- to full-bodied wine marked by dark plum and wild-berry fruit, an herbal, almost savoury edge, firm acidity and sturdy tannins.

**Where it grows** — Friuli-Venezia Giulia is its home, with plantings also across the border in Slovenia and scattered elsewhere; cooler sites keep it fresh and tightly wound, warmer ones round it into something plusher.

**At the table** — A natural match for grilled and roasted red meats, game and hearty pasta dishes.

**Cellaring** — Its acidity and tannin let it age gracefully for several years, softening and gaining complexity, though it is also enjoyable young.

name: Roditis
description:
**Roditis** is a white (pink-skinned) grape widely grown across Greece, with a strong presence in the Peloponnese, where it is a cornerstone of everyday and fine white wines alike.

**In the glass** — It tends toward a pale, lightly golden wine with citrus, melon and delicate floral notes, a fresh lively acidity and a light to medium body.

**Where it grows** — Found throughout mainland Greece, it is closely tied to the Patras area of the northern Peloponnese, and higher-altitude vineyards give crisper, more mineral results than warmer lowland sites.

**At the table** — A fine partner for grilled fish, seafood, salads and lemony Mediterranean fare.

**Cellaring** — Best enjoyed young and fresh, though carefully grown, low-yield versions can hold a little longer.

name: Trebbiano
description:
**Trebbiano** is a white grape and one of Italy's most widely planted, actually a family of related varieties responsible for oceans of everyday white wine as well as the base for balsamic vinegar and brandy.

**In the glass** — Typically pale and light-bodied, it offers gentle citrus and orchard-fruit aromas, a clean neutral character and refreshing, sometimes sharp acidity.

**Where it grows** — It is grown up and down Italy under many local names, and as Ugni Blanc it is hugely important in France, especially for distillation into Cognac and Armagnac; the style stays fresh and unassuming across regions.

**At the table** — An easy match for light seafood, antipasti and simple everyday dishes.

**Cellaring** — Made to be drunk young and fresh; only rare, ambitious examples reward keeping.

name: Albillo
description:
**Albillo** is a white grape from Spain, associated in particular with the Castilla region of the central plateau, where it is prized for its aromatic, textured whites.

**In the glass** — It gives a pale, medium-bodied wine with white-flower, orchard-fruit and subtle nutty notes, a smooth, slightly glyceric texture and moderate acidity.

**Where it grows** — Central Spain is its stronghold, notably around the Sierra de Gredos and Castilla areas, where old bush vines at altitude yield concentrated, mineral-tinged whites; it is sometimes also blended into local reds to soften them.

**At the table** — Good with roast poultry, pork, creamy dishes and mild cheeses.

**Cellaring** — Generally best in its youth, though the finest old-vine bottlings can develop attractively over a few years.

name: Cesanese d'Affile
description:
**Cesanese d'Affile** is a red grape from the Lazio region around Rome, taking its name from the town of Affile; it is the more prized, smaller-berried member of the Cesanese group and central to the area's best reds.

**In the glass** — Expect a medium-bodied, perfumed wine of red cherry and dark berry fruit lifted by floral and spicy notes, with soft-to-firm tannins and a warm, gently rustic feel.

**Where it grows** — Its home is the hills southeast of Rome, where it anchors appellations such as Cesanese del Piglio; site and vintage swing it between bright and juicy or deeper and more structured.

**At the table** — Pairs well with roast lamb, cured meats and tomato-rich Roman cooking.

**Cellaring** — Enjoyable young but the more serious examples gain complexity over several years.

name: Sagrantino
description:
**Sagrantino** is a red grape from the Umbria region of central Italy, centred on the town of Montefalco, and is famous as one of the most tannic varieties in the world.

**In the glass** — It yields a deep, inky, full-bodied wine of blackberry and dark plum with notes of tar, spice and dried herbs, built on powerful, muscular tannins and firm acidity.

**Where it grows** — Montefalco in Umbria is its near-exclusive home, where it makes both the dry, age-worthy Montefalco Sagrantino and a traditional sweet passito from dried grapes.

**At the table** — Made for rich, fatty dishes — braised and grilled red meats, game and hard aged cheeses.

**Cellaring** — Its formidable tannin demands time; the best dry versions can age and mellow for a decade or more.

name: Grechetto
description:
**Grechetto** is a white grape most closely tied to Umbria in central Italy, where it is a mainstay of the region's whites both on its own and in blends.

**In the glass** — It offers a medium-bodied wine with pear, white-flower and gently nutty aromas, a subtle almond twist on the finish and fresh, well-balanced acidity.

**Where it grows** — Umbria is its heartland, notably around Orvieto and Torgiano, and it also turns up in neighbouring parts of central Italy; it can be made crisp and unoaked or given more texture and body.

**At the table** — A versatile match for antipasti, fish, poultry and vegetable dishes.

**Cellaring** — Best enjoyed within a few years, though richer, more structured styles keep a little longer.

name: Johanniter
description:
**Johanniter** is a white grape and a modern disease-resistant (PIWI) hybrid bred in Germany, developed from Riesling and other varieties to combine quality with resilience in the vineyard.

**In the glass** — It leans on its Riesling parentage, showing green-apple and citrus fruit, a floral lift and crisp, refreshing acidity in a light to medium body.

**Where it grows** — Planted mainly in Germany and other cooler parts of central and northern Europe, it appeals to growers seeking lower-spray, more sustainable viticulture without sacrificing freshness.

**At the table** — Good with light fish, salads, soft cheeses and lightly spiced dishes.

**Cellaring** — Generally best young and fresh, when its bright acidity and aromatics are at their most appealing.

name: Cesanese Comune
description:
**Cesanese Comune** is a red grape from the Lazio region around Rome, and — as its name suggests — the more common, larger-berried and more widely planted member of the Cesanese family (often simply called Cesanese).

**In the glass** — It produces a medium-bodied red with red-cherry and berry fruit, a floral, faintly spicy character, soft tannins and a warm, approachable feel.

**Where it grows** — Its home is the hills of southeastern Lazio, where it contributes to the region's Cesanese-based appellations, sometimes alongside its finer cousin Cesanese d'Affile.

**At the table** — Pairs happily with roast meats, cured pork and rustic Roman dishes.

**Cellaring** — Usually best enjoyed young and fruity, within a few years of the vintage.

name: Maréchal Foch
description:
**Maréchal Foch** is a red grape, a French-bred hybrid created in the early twentieth century that has found much of its home in the cooler wine regions of North America.

**In the glass** — It gives a deeply coloured, medium-bodied wine of dark berry and plum fruit with earthy, sometimes smoky notes, bright acidity and generally soft tannins.

**Where it grows** — Once grown in France, it is now most associated with Canada and the northern and eastern United States, where its hardiness and early ripening suit short, cold-climate growing seasons.

**At the table** — Works well with grilled meats, burgers, barbecue and hearty casual fare.

**Cellaring** — Most versions are made for early drinking, though riper, oak-aged bottlings can hold for a few years.

name: Chambourcin
description:
**Chambourcin** is a red French-American hybrid grape, bred in France and now planted mainly across the eastern and midwestern United States, where its resistance to fungal disease makes it valuable in humid climates.

**In the glass** — it shows a deep, almost inky ruby-purple, with aromas of dark berries and plum often carrying a leafy, herbal edge; the palate is medium-bodied with moderate, supple tannin and lively acidity.

**Where it grows** — it is a workhorse in states like Missouri, Pennsylvania, Illinois and New York, and turns up in Australia and its native France; warmer sites push it toward riper fruit, while cooler ones emphasise its green, savoury side.

**At the table** — a natural match for grilled meats and barbecue.

**Cellaring** — generally best enjoyed within a few years, though sturdier examples can hold for a while.

name: Blauer Portugieser
description:
**Blauer Portugieser** is a red grape long grown across Austria and Central Europe, prized for high yields and easy, unfussy drinking despite a name that has little real connection to Portugal.

**In the glass** — expect a pale-to-medium ruby, soft red-cherry and berry fruit, a light body, gentle tannin and moderate acidity that make it approachable and refreshing.

**Where it grows** — it is widespread in Austria's Weinviertel and other northern regions, in German areas such as the Pfalz, Rheinhessen and Ahr, and in Hungary, where it is known as Kékoportó; everywhere the aim is fruity, early-drinking wine rather than depth.

**At the table** — good with charcuterie, lighter meats and casual fare.

**Cellaring** — made to be drunk young and fresh.

name: Malvasia Nera
description:
**Malvasia Nera** is a red member of the large and aromatic Malvasia family, associated above all with southern Italy and the region of Puglia.

**In the glass** — it is prized for perfume: floral, violet-scented aromas over ripe red berries and a hint of spice, with a medium body and soft, rounded tannins.

**Where it grows** — Puglia is its heartland, where it is often blended in small amounts with Negroamaro to lift the fragrance of wines like Salice Salentino; it also appears elsewhere in central and southern Italy, where several distinct sub-varieties share the name.

**At the table** — try it with tomato-based pasta, roast lamb or grilled vegetables.

**Cellaring** — mostly enjoyed young for its aromatics, though structured blends can hold for a few years.

name: Arinto dos Açores
description:
**Arinto dos Açores** is a white grape native to Portugal's Azores, and especially the volcanic island of Pico, where vines grow in tiny stone-walled plots amid black basalt.

**In the glass** — it is defined by tension and salinity: pale colour, citrus and mineral aromas, a distinctly saline, ocean-swept character, and bracing high acidity over a light-to-medium body.

**Where it grows** — it is bound to the maritime, volcanic Azores rather than the mainland, and it is a separate variety from the more familiar Arinto grown near Lisbon.

**At the table** — made for shellfish, oysters and fresh seafood.

**Cellaring** — lovely young, but its firm acidity gives the best examples real ageing potential.

name: Albillo Mayor
description:
**Albillo Mayor** is a white grape of north-central Spain, most closely tied to Ribera del Duero, where it is the traditional white companion to the region's dominant red Tempranillo.

**In the glass** — it offers a pale colour, gentle white-flower and orchard-fruit aromas and a rounded texture, with medium acidity and a soft, approachable body.

**Where it grows** — it is centred on Ribera del Duero and neighbouring areas of Castilla y León; historically it was even added in small amounts to red blends, and today it increasingly appears as a characterful white in its own right.

**At the table** — pairs well with white fish, poultry and lighter dishes.

**Cellaring** — usually enjoyed young, though barrel-aged or skin-contact styles can develop over several years.

name: Antão Vaz
description:
**Antão Vaz** is a white grape at home in the hot, dry Alentejo region of southern Portugal, valued for ripening reliably and holding its shape in a demanding climate.

**In the glass** — it tends toward ripe citrus, tropical fruit and stone-fruit flavours, with a full, generous body and moderate acidity that keeps it from feeling heavy.

**Where it grows** — the Alentejo is its stronghold, both as a varietal wine and as a backbone in regional blends; it is planted increasingly across Portugal for its dependable ripeness and structure.

**At the table** — a good partner for grilled fish, richer seafood and roast pork.

**Cellaring** — mostly drunk young, but oak-aged versions can gain complexity over a few years.

name: Roupeiro
description:
**Roupeiro** is a white grape widely grown in Portugal's Alentejo, where it is also known as Síria (and appears as Códega in the Douro).

**In the glass** — when young it is charmingly aromatic, showing citrus, white flowers and soft peach over a light-to-medium body and moderate acidity.

**Where it grows** — it is common across the Alentejo and inland central Portugal; its main challenge is heat, which can cause it to lose freshness quickly, so it is at its best from cooler sites and early picking.

**At the table** — suits light fish dishes, salads and fresh cheeses.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed young while its aromatics are lively.

name: Moscato
description:
**Moscato** is the Italian name for the white Muscat grape, above all the ancient Moscato Bianco (Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains), and it is one of the most instantly recognisable, floral grapes in the world.

**In the glass** — it is unmistakably grapey and perfumed, with orange blossom, ripe peach and honeysuckle; most famously it is made lightly sweet and gently sparkling, low in alcohol, with bright acidity keeping it fresh rather than cloying.

**Where it grows** — Piedmont is its most celebrated home, source of the frothy, fragrant Moscato d'Asti and sparkling Asti, but it is planted throughout Italy and, as Muscat, across the wine world in styles from dry to richly sweet.

**At the table** — delightful with fresh fruit, light desserts, or simply as a low-alcohol aperitif.

**Cellaring** — meant to be drunk young, while its aromatics are at their most vivid.

name: Molette
description:
**Molette** is a white grape of the Savoie region in the French Alps, associated in particular with the town of Seyssel.

**In the glass** — it is delicate and understated, offering subtle floral and citrus notes, a light body and the crisp, high acidity typical of mountain whites.

**Where it grows** — it is essentially local to Savoie and Seyssel, where it is often blended with the more aromatic Altesse (Roussette) and used as a base for the region's sparkling wines.

**At the table** — a natural match for alpine cheeses and freshwater fish.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed young and fresh.

name: Muskat Ottonel
description:
**Muskat Ottonel** is a white member of the Muscat family, created in France's Loire around the middle of the 19th century and now most at home in Austria and Central Europe.

**In the glass** — it is the most delicate and elegant of the Muscats, with gentle orange-blossom, grape and floral aromas, a light body and moderate acidity; it can be made bone dry or lusciously sweet.

**Where it grows** — it thrives in Austria, Alsace, and across Hungary, Romania and the Balkans, ripening early and giving fragrant wines that lean more floral than intensely grapey.

**At the table** — a fine aperitif, good with lightly spiced dishes, or with fruit desserts in its sweeter form.

**Cellaring** — dry styles are best young, while sweet late-harvest versions can age gracefully.

name: Rieslaner
description:
**Rieslaner** is a white German crossing of Silvaner and Riesling, developed in Franken in the early 20th century and prized for the intensity and racy acidity it inherits.

**In the glass** — it delivers vivid citrus and stone fruit, taking on honeyed richness in sweeter versions, all carried by a bright, mouth-watering acidity and medium body.

**Where it grows** — it remains a specialty of Franken and the Pfalz in Germany, where it needs warm, favoured sites to ripen fully and shines in concentrated, botrytis-influenced dessert wines.

**At the table** — dry examples suit rich fish and poultry, while sweet ones pair beautifully with fruit tarts or blue cheese.

**Cellaring** — the great sweet wines can age for decades, though dry styles are best within a few years.

name: Chasselas
description:
**Chasselas** is a white grape most closely tied to the shores of Lake Geneva in Switzerland, where it is the country's signature white; in Germany's Baden it goes by the name Gutedel.

**In the glass** — It is famously understated, offering gentle notes of orchard fruit, white flowers and a chalky, sometimes faintly smoky character, with modest acidity, light body and a subtle salinity rather than showy fruit.

**Where it grows** — Switzerland is its heartland, especially Vaud (Lavaux and La Côte) and Valais, where steep lakeside terraces let it mirror the soil beneath it. It also appears in Alsace, along the upper Loire around Pouilly-sur-Loire, in Germany as Gutedel, and it is widely grown as a table grape.

**At the table** — A natural partner for cheese fondue, raclette and freshwater fish.

**Cellaring** — Most versions are made to be drunk young and fresh, though the finest Swiss crus from good sites can gain texture and depth over several years.

name: Moschofilero
description:
**Moschofilero** is a white (technically pink-skinned) aromatic grape from Greece, with its home in the high plateau of Mantinia in the central Peloponnese.

**In the glass** — It is intensely perfumed in the Muscat mould, with rose petal, orange blossom and spice lifting from a pale, sometimes faintly copper-tinged wine; the palate is crisp and lively, with bright acidity, light body and a fragrant, slightly bitter finish.

**Where it grows** — Mantinia, sitting at altitude in the Peloponnese, is its stronghold and gives the coolest, most floral expression. It is grown more broadly across Greece for aromatic dry whites and occasional pink and sparkling styles.

**At the table** — Lovely with grilled seafood, herb-flecked salads and lighter Mediterranean dishes.

**Cellaring** — Best enjoyed young while its aromatics are at their most vivid.

name: Lambrusco
description:
**Lambrusco** is a red grape, or really a family of related varieties, native to Emilia-Romagna in northern Italy, famous for producing lightly sparkling red wine.

**In the glass** — Expect a vivid purple wine topped with a frothy pink foam, scented with red cherry, blackberry and violets; it is typically frizzante, with fresh acidity, light-to-moderate tannin and a juicy, drinkable feel, made in styles from bone-dry (secco) to sweet (dolce).

**Where it grows** — The area around Modena and Reggio Emilia is its base, home to distinct subvarieties such as Grasparossa, Salamino and Sorbara, each shifting the colour, structure and fizz.

**At the table** — A classic foil for the region's rich fare — cured meats, Parmigiano and lasagne.

**Cellaring** — Made for immediate, chilled enjoyment; drink it young and bubbly.

name: Vitovska
description:
**Vitovska** is a white grape from the windswept Carso limestone plateau that straddles the border between Friuli in northeastern Italy and Slovenia's Kras.

**In the glass** — It shows delicate white flowers, pear and herbs with a distinct saline, stony edge; the palate is dry and firmly acidic with a light-to-medium body, and it is a favourite for skin-macerated "orange" wines that add grip and amber colour.

**Where it grows** — Its natural home is the Carso/Kras, where thin soils over rock and coastal winds shape a lean, mineral style. Plantings remain small and locally focused, championed by a handful of dedicated growers.

**At the table** — Pairs well with cured ham, seafood and vegetable dishes.

**Cellaring** — Fresh versions drink well young, while structured and skin-contact bottlings can develop over several years.

name: Carricante
description:
**Carricante** is a white grape native to the volcanic slopes of Mount Etna in Sicily, and the backbone of the region's crisp, age-worthy whites.

**In the glass** — It is bracing and mineral, with green apple, citrus, white flowers and a smoky, flinty character drawn from the volcanic soils; high acidity, a lean-to-medium body and a saline, sometimes almost anise-tinged finish define it.

**Where it grows** — Etna is its home, where old vines on high, ash-rich terraces give the finest Etna Bianco, often at considerable altitude. It is grown almost entirely in eastern Sicily.

**At the table** — Excellent with shellfish, grilled fish and lighter poultry.

**Cellaring** — Unusually for a white, the best examples reward patience, gaining honeyed, nutty complexity with several years in bottle.

name: Albanello
description:
**Albanello** is a white grape from Sicily, historically associated with the southeastern corner of the island.

**In the glass** — It generally gives a dry white of moderate weight with orchard and citrus fruit and fresh acidity; it has also been used historically for richer, sweeter styles.

**Where it grows** — It is a local Sicilian variety, now quite rare and grown only in small quantities.

**At the table** — A versatile companion to seafood and lighter dishes.

**Cellaring** — Best enjoyed young in its dry form.

name: Piedirosso
description:
**Piedirosso** is a red grape from Campania in southern Italy, whose name ("red foot") nods to the reddish stalks of its bunches; it is a traditional partner to Aglianico.

**In the glass** — It leans toward red cherry, cranberry and dried herbs with an earthy, sometimes volcanic edge; the palate is medium-bodied with soft, gentle tannins and moderate acidity, making it approachable and savoury rather than powerful.

**Where it grows** — Campania is its home, from the slopes of Vesuvius and the volcanic Campi Flegrei to the Amalfi coast, where it appears both on its own and softening the firmer Aglianico in regional blends.

**At the table** — Good with pizza, tomato-based pasta and grilled vegetables.

**Cellaring** — Generally best enjoyed within a few years, while its fruit stays bright.

name: Sciascinoso
description:
**Sciascinoso** is a red grape from Campania in southern Italy, sometimes known locally as Olivella.

**In the glass** — It offers soft red-berry fruit with an earthy undertone, a medium body and moderate, supple tannins, which suits it to a gentle supporting role.

**Where it grows** — It is a Campanian variety, most often used as a minor blending partner alongside grapes such as Aglianico and Piedirosso rather than bottled on its own.

**At the table** — Pairs comfortably with everyday pasta, pizza and grilled fare.

**Cellaring** — Best enjoyed young and fresh.

name: Rossese Bianco
description:
**Rossese Bianco** is a white grape associated with Piedmont in northwestern Italy.

**In the glass** — It tends to give a light, dry white with delicate orchard and floral notes and fresh acidity.

**Where it grows** — It is a rare local variety grown in small amounts in Piedmont; despite the shared name it is distinct from the red Rossese of Liguria.

**At the table** — Suits antipasti, seafood and lighter dishes.

**Cellaring** — Best enjoyed young while fresh.

name: Durella
description:
**Durella** is a white grape from the Lessini hills of the Veneto in northern Italy, prized above all for its firm acidity.

**In the glass** — It is taut and racy, showing green apple, citrus, white flowers and a flinty, sometimes almondy note; the searing acidity, light body and mineral cut make it a natural base for sparkling wine.

**Where it grows** — Its stronghold is the volcanic Lessini terrain around the Verona–Vicenza border, where the traditional and tank methods turn it into the crisp sparkling wine known as Lessini Durello.

**At the table** — Excellent as an aperitif and with fried seafood or salty snacks.

**Cellaring** — Sparkling versions drink well young, though the tension of longer-aged, traditional-method bottlings can develop attractively over time.

name: Pelaverga Piccolo
description:
**Pelaverga Piccolo** is a red grape from Piedmont in northwestern Italy, closely tied to the village of Verduno in the Barolo zone, where it makes a charming, distinctive light red.

**In the glass** — It is pale and perfumed, with red berries, rose and a signature dusting of white pepper and spice; the palate is light-bodied with fine, gentle tannins and lively acidity, fresh and easy to drink.

**Where it grows** — Its home is Verduno and a few neighbouring communes in the Langhe, where the Verduno Pelaverga appellation showcases its peppery, fragrant character. Plantings are small and highly local.

**At the table** — A delight with charcuterie, lighter meats and, served slightly cool, a range of everyday dishes.

**Cellaring** — Made to be enjoyed young while its aromatic spice and freshness shine.

name: Colorino
description:
**Colorino** is a red grape from Tuscany in central Italy, prized less as a solo performer than as a supporting player that lends deep pigment to blends. Its name literally nods to colour, and it has long been a traditional seasoning grape in Chianti and other Sangiovese-based wines.
