**In the glass** — it pours an intense, almost inky ruby-purple, with dark berry and plummy notes, firm tannins and moderate acidity. On its own it can feel a touch rustic and compact rather than perfumed.

**Where it grows** — it is very much a Tuscan speciality, planted in small amounts across Chianti and the surrounding hills, where growers add a splash to boost colour and grip in Sangiovese blends. Varietal bottlings are rare but do exist.

**At the table** — pair it with hearty ragù, grilled meats or aged pecorino.

**Cellaring** — its colour and tannin give blends staying power, though as a standalone wine it is usually best enjoyed within a few years.

name: Azal
description:
**Azal** is a white grape from the Vinho Verde region in the northwest of Portugal, one of the traditional varieties behind that area's fresh, lightly spritzy wines. It ripens late and thrives in the cool, damp Atlantic climate of the Minho.

**In the glass** — expect a pale, bright wine with zesty green-apple and citrus aromas, racy high acidity and a light body, sometimes with a gentle prickle of carbon dioxide.

**Where it grows** — it is closely tied to Vinho Verde, where it is often blended with grapes like Loureiro, Arinto and Trajadura to make crisp, low-alcohol whites, though it is increasingly bottled on its own.

**At the table** — a natural match for grilled sardines, shellfish and other Atlantic seafood.

**Cellaring** — this is a wine to drink young and fresh, ideally within a year or two of the vintage.

name: Tressallier
description:
**Tressallier** is a white grape grown in the Saint-Pourçain area of central France, in the Allier, where it is the local name for the variety more widely known as Sacy. It gives the region's white wines a distinctive, home-grown character.

**In the glass** — it produces pale, light-bodied whites with brisk acidity and delicate citrus, orchard-fruit and floral notes, generally more about freshness than power.

**Where it grows** — its stronghold is Saint-Pourçain, where it is often blended with Chardonnay and sometimes Sauvignon Blanc to soften its sharp edges and add roundness. Plantings outside the region are limited.

**At the table** — serve it well chilled with river fish, goat cheese or light starters.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed young while its crisp, lively acidity is at its peak.

name: Asprinio di Aversa
description:
**Asprinio di Aversa** is a white grape from Campania in southern Italy, famous for the dramatic way it is trained up tall trees and pergolas in the Aversa plain north of Naples. Its name comes from the Italian for sharp or tart, a fitting clue to its style.

**In the glass** — it is bracingly acidic and light, with a pale colour, lemon and green-apple aromas and a lean, mineral finish, which makes it a natural base for sparkling wines.

**Where it grows** — it is essentially a Campanian speciality centred on Aversa, where it appears both as a still white and, more famously, as a crisp traditional-method or lightly fizzy sparkler.

**At the table** — it cuts beautifully through fried seafood, mozzarella and antipasti.

**Cellaring** — drink it young, when its high acidity and freshness are most appealing.

name: Plavac Mali
description:
**Plavac Mali** is a red grape from the Dalmatian coast of Croatia and the country's most important native red. Genetics have shown it to be a natural offspring of Tribidrag crossed with the local Dobričić, and because Tribidrag is the very same variety Californians call Zinfandel and Italians call Primitivo, Plavac Mali is a direct descendant of that famous grape.

**In the glass** — it gives deeply coloured, full-bodied wines that are high in alcohol, with dark cherry, fig and dried-plum fruit, warm spice, firm tannins and a sometimes slightly rustic grip.

**Where it grows** — it flourishes on the steep, sun-baked slopes and stony islands of southern Dalmatia, with the Dingač and Postup sites on the Pelješac peninsula producing its most powerful and celebrated wines.

**At the table** — pair it with grilled lamb, hearty stews and rich braised meats.

**Cellaring** — the top examples have real tannin and concentration and can age well for several years, softening and deepening with time.

name: Plavina
description:
**Plavina** is a red grape native to the Dalmatian coast of Croatia, valued as a reliable, productive workhorse that yields approachable everyday reds. It is often found alongside more prestigious local varieties in the region's vineyards.

**In the glass** — it tends toward a lighter, paler style, with soft red-cherry and berry fruit, gentle tannins and moderate acidity, giving easy-drinking, unpretentious wines.

**Where it grows** — it is widely planted throughout coastal Dalmatia, where it is frequently blended with grapes such as Plavac Mali and Babić to add softness and drinkability, though varietal versions exist too.

**At the table** — it suits grilled fish, cured meats and simple Mediterranean fare.

**Cellaring** — this is a wine to drink young while its fruit is fresh and its tannins supple.

name: Lasina
description:
**Lasina** is a red grape from the Dalmatian coast of Croatia, also known as Lasin, one of the many indigenous varieties of the region. It is a minor grape kept alive largely by tradition and local growers.

**In the glass** — it typically gives lighter-bodied reds with fresh red-fruit character, modest tannins and lively acidity.

**Where it grows** — it is found in small amounts in coastal Dalmatia, where it is often used as a blending component rather than bottled on its own.

**At the table** — it pairs happily with grilled fish and light Mediterranean dishes.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed young and fresh.

name: Babić
description:
**Babić** is a red grape from the Dalmatian coast of Croatia, closely associated with the rugged limestone slopes around the town of Primošten. It is one of Dalmatia's more characterful and structured native reds.

**In the glass** — it produces deeply coloured, medium- to full-bodied wines with dark cherry and berry fruit, a peppery, herbal edge, firm tannins and refreshing acidity, especially from low-yielding vines on stony ground.

**Where it grows** — its heartland is the karst vineyards near Primošten and Šibenik, where poor soils and coastal sun concentrate the fruit; it is also grown more widely along the Dalmatian coast.

**At the table** — it stands up well to grilled and roasted red meats, game and hard cheeses.

**Cellaring** — the more serious, concentrated examples have the structure to develop over several years in the cellar.

name: Gaglioppo
description:
**Gaglioppo** is a red grape from Calabria in the far south of Italy, where it is the driving force behind the region's best-known reds, above all those of Cirò. It has long been the signature dark grape of the Calabrian coast.

**In the glass** — it gives medium-bodied wines that can be surprisingly pale for a southern red, with red-cherry and dried-herb aromas, a savoury, slightly earthy character, firm tannins and notably fresh acidity.

**Where it grows** — it is centred on Calabria, especially the Cirò zone along the Ionian coast, where warm sun and coastal breezes shape its mix of ripeness and freshness. Styles range from traditional and structured to more modern and fruit-forward.

**At the table** — pair it with grilled lamb, spicy sausage and tomato-based pasta.

**Cellaring** — its tannin and acidity allow the better wines to age and mellow gracefully over several years.

name: Alarije
description:
**Alarije** is a white grape grown in the Extremadura region of western Spain, one of the traditional varieties of that warm, inland area. It is a local grape with a limited footprint beyond its home ground.

**In the glass** — it tends to give light- to medium-bodied whites with gentle orchard-fruit and floral notes and moderate acidity, suited to easy, everyday drinking.

**Where it grows** — it is planted mainly in Extremadura, where it contributes to the region's white wines, sometimes on its own and sometimes as part of a blend.

**At the table** — serve it chilled with light tapas, poultry or fresh cheeses.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed young while it is fresh and fruity.

name: Sciacarello
description:
**Sciacarello** is a red grape native to the island of Corsica, where it is one of the traditional varieties that give the local wines their distinct Mediterranean identity. It is especially associated with the granite hills around Ajaccio.

**In the glass** — despite being a red grape it yields relatively pale, light- to medium-bodied wines, marked by red-fruit and berry aromas, a peppery, spicy character and a fresh, savoury finish; it also makes appealing rosés.

**Where it grows** — it is centred on the western side of Corsica, particularly the Ajaccio and Sartène areas, where the island's granitic soils and warm, breezy climate suit it well.

**At the table** — it pairs nicely with grilled meats, charcuterie and herb-scented Mediterranean dishes.

**Cellaring** — generally best enjoyed in its fresh, fragrant youth, though the more structured examples can hold for a few years.

name: Muscaris
description:
**Muscaris** is a white grape bred in Germany by crossing Solaris with a Muscat variety, developed as a modern PIWI (fungus-resistant) grape that lets growers cut back sharply on spraying.

**In the glass** — it is unmistakably aromatic, giving fragrant notes of ripe muscat grapes, orange blossom, elderflower and citrus, with a soft, fruity palate and gentle acidity. It works both dry and in off-dry or sweeter styles.

**Where it grows** — plantings are still small and concentrated in German-speaking wine countries such as Germany, Austria and Switzerland, where organic and low-intervention growers favour its disease resistance; it also appears in newer cool-climate regions experimenting with resistant varieties.

**At the table** — lovely as an aperitif or with lightly spiced Asian dishes and fresh fruit.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed young while its perfumed aromatics are at their most vivid.

name: Charbono
description:
**Charbono** is a red grape of French origin, known in the Savoie region as Douce Noir, and the same variety travelled to become Bonarda in Argentina and Charbono in California.

**In the glass** — it makes deeply coloured, dark-fruited wines with plum and blackberry, brisk acidity, and moderate but firm tannins, typically medium to full in body.

**Where it grows** — its Alpine French homeland is small, but it found a wider stage in Argentina (as one of the country's most-planted reds under the Bonarda name) and holds a cult niche among a handful of California growers who keep it alive.

**At the table** — a natural with grilled red meats, sausages and hearty stews.

**Cellaring** — approachable young, though the firmer, more structured examples can reward several years in the cellar.

name: Mavro Kalavrytino
description:
**Mavro Kalavrytino** is a red grape from Greece, associated with the Kalavryta area in the mountainous Achaia region of the northern Peloponnese. Its name simply means "black grape of Kalavryta."

**In the glass** — it tends toward a paler, lighter-bodied red with red-berry fruit, fresh acidity and modest tannin, in keeping with its cool, high-altitude home.

**Where it grows** — it is a local speciality, rare outside its native corner of Achaia, and cultivated by a small number of Greek growers keeping regional heritage varieties in production.

**At the table** — pairs happily with lighter meat dishes, grilled vegetables and Mediterranean fare.

**Cellaring** — generally made to be drunk young and fresh rather than aged.

name: Mavrud
description:
**Mavrud** is a red grape native to Bulgaria and closely tied to the Thracian Lowlands, where it stands as one of the country's flagship indigenous varieties with a long local history.

**In the glass** — it is deeply coloured and full-bodied, offering dark berries, plum and often a savoury, spicy edge, framed by substantial tannin and good acidity that give the wines real grip.

**Where it grows** — it is grown almost entirely in Bulgaria, above all in the warmer southern Thracian regions that suit its late ripening, and it is a point of national pride for Bulgarian producers.

**At the table** — excellent with slow-cooked lamb, grilled meats and rich stews.

**Cellaring** — its firm structure makes it well suited to ageing, with the best examples softening and deepening over a number of years.

name: Black Muscat
description:
**Black Muscat** is a dark-skinned grape, also known as Muscat of Hamburg, bred in England as a Muscat crossing that marries Muscat perfume with deep colour; it is used both as a table grape and for sweet wines.

**In the glass** — it is intensely perfumed, with rose petal, violet and ripe grape notes, and in its classic dessert form gives a lush, sweet, softly structured wine of deep hue.

**Where it grows** — beyond its English origins it is best known today in California, where it is bottled as a fortified or late-harvest sweet wine, and it turns up more broadly as an eating grape.

**At the table** — a natural match for chocolate desserts, berry tarts and blue cheese.

**Cellaring** — the sweet versions can hold for years, though most of their floral charm shows early.

name: Melon de Bourgogne
description:
**Melon de Bourgogne** is a white grape that originated in Burgundy but found its true home in the western Loire, where it is the sole grape of Muscadet near the Atlantic coast.

**In the glass** — it is famously restrained and dry, with subtle citrus and green-apple notes, a saline, mineral edge and crisp, refreshing acidity; the best examples gain body and texture from ageing on the lees (sur lie).

**Where it grows** — it is overwhelmingly a Loire Valley variety around Nantes, with only scattered plantings elsewhere, thriving in the cool, maritime climate and often stony soils.

**At the table** — the classic partner for oysters, shellfish and other seafood.

**Cellaring** — usually enjoyed young, though serious lees-aged Muscadet from top crus can develop beautifully over a decade.

name: Timorasso
description:
**Timorasso** is a white grape from the Piedmont region of Italy, centred on the Colli Tortonesi hills, and a variety rescued from near-extinction to become one of northern Italy's most exciting whites.

**In the glass** — it produces structured, full-bodied wines with citrus, orchard fruit, honey and a distinctive stony, mineral character, backed by firm acidity that gives it length and drive.

**Where it grows** — it is almost entirely a Piedmontese speciality of the Tortona hills, where it is often bottled under the name Derthona, and its revival has been driven by a dedicated group of local growers.

**At the table** — good with rich fish dishes, poultry, risotto and mature cheeses.

**Cellaring** — one of Italy's more age-worthy whites, gaining complexity and nutty depth over several years.

name: Vidiano
description:
**Vidiano** is a white grape native to the island of Crete in Greece, a long-overlooked local variety now at the heart of the island's white-wine renaissance.

**In the glass** — it is aromatic yet balanced, offering ripe stone fruit such as apricot and peach, subtle floral and almond notes, a rounded, medium-bodied palate and moderate, well-judged acidity.

**Where it grows** — it is grown almost exclusively on Crete, where warm Mediterranean conditions suit it, and Cretan producers have championed it as a signature grape of the island.

**At the table** — a fine match for grilled fish, roast poultry and herb-driven Mediterranean cooking.

**Cellaring** — enjoyable young, though its texture and depth mean better examples can hold and develop for a few years.

name: Rkatsiteli
description:
**Rkatsiteli** is a white grape from Georgia, especially the eastern Kakheti region, and one of the world's oldest and most widely planted traditional varieties, central to the country's ancient winemaking heritage.

**In the glass** — it is marked by bright, firm acidity with green-apple and citrus fruit and a subtle spicy, floral character; when fermented on the skins in traditional clay qvevri it turns amber, gaining tannin, nuttiness and dried-fruit depth.

**Where it grows** — Georgia remains its heartland, but it is also grown across Eastern Europe and the former Soviet countries, and in pockets of the United States.

**At the table** — versatile with white meats, vegetable dishes and, in its amber form, robust and spiced fare.

**Cellaring** — fresh styles drink young, while skin-contact qvevri versions can age impressively for many years.

name: Mtsvane
description:
**Mtsvane** is a white grape from Georgia, grown notably in the eastern Kakheti region, whose name means "green" in reference to its greenish berries; it is a prized part of the country's indigenous winemaking tradition.

**In the glass** — it is delicately aromatic, with floral, orchard-fruit and stone-fruit notes and lively acidity; vinified traditionally on the skins in qvevri it takes on amber colour, grip and greater complexity.

**Where it grows** — it is essentially a Georgian variety, most at home in Kakheti, where it is often blended with Rkatsiteli to lift aromatics.

**At the table** — pairs well with herbed vegetable dishes, white meats and Georgian cuisine.

**Cellaring** — fresh examples are best young, while skin-contact versions gain the structure to age for several years.

name: Solaris
description:
**Solaris** is a white grape bred in Germany in the 1970s as a PIWI (fungus-resistant) crossing, prized for ripening very early and reaching high sugar levels with little need for spraying.

**In the glass** — it gives ripe, fruity wines with notes of pineapple, peach and citrus, a full, generous palate and often relatively soft acidity; it can be made dry or in richer sweet styles.

**Where it grows** — its disease resistance and early ripening have made it a cornerstone of cool- and cold-climate viticulture, planted in Germany, Scandinavia, England, Belgium and the Netherlands where classic varieties struggle to ripen.

**At the table** — good as an aperitif or with light fish, salads and soft cheeses.

**Cellaring** — generally best enjoyed young while its fresh fruit is at its peak.

name: Avgoustiatis
description:
**Avgoustiatis** is a red grape from Greece, most closely tied to the Ionian island of Zakynthos, where it is the local red of note. Its name comes from the Greek word for August, the month with which the grape has long been associated.

**In the glass** — it pours a deep, saturated red and shows ripe red and dark berry fruit, sometimes with a spicy or herbal edge. The palate is medium-bodied with fresh acidity and soft, approachable tannins.

**Where it grows** — Zakynthos is its heartland, with scattered plantings elsewhere in western Greece and around the wider Ionian and Aegean. It is usually vinified as a dry red, occasionally in richer or sweeter styles, and sometimes blended with other local varieties.

**At the table** — a natural match for grilled lamb, roasted vegetables and tomato-based Mediterranean dishes.

**Cellaring** — generally at its best young and fruit-forward, though more structured bottlings can hold for a few years.

name: Boğazkere
description:
**Boğazkere** is a red grape from southeastern Anatolia in Turkey, prized as one of the country's most serious indigenous varieties. Its name roughly translates as "throat burner," a vivid warning about its formidable grip.

**In the glass** — it is deeply coloured and firmly tannic, with dark fruit, dried plum and a savoury, sometimes leathery or spicy character. Full-bodied with real structure, it can be austere in youth.

**Where it grows** — its traditional home is the area around Diyarbakır in southeastern Turkey, though it is planted more widely across Anatolia. Because of its tannic power it is very often blended with the softer, juicier Öküzgözü to bring balance.

**At the table** — pair it with grilled and roasted red meats, kebabs and hearty stews.

**Cellaring** — its tannin and structure reward patience, and good examples soften and develop over several years in the cellar.

name: Caíño Tinto
description:
**Caíño Tinto** is a red grape from Galicia in northwestern Spain, part of a small family of old Iberian varieties grown along the Atlantic. It has long been a traditional presence in the region's cool, damp vineyards.

**In the glass** — it is marked by bright, mouth-watering acidity and firm tannins, with tart red fruit, a floral lift and an earthy, savoury undertone. Wines tend to be medium-bodied and vibrant rather than plush.

**Where it grows** — it is most at home in Galician appellations such as Rías Baixas and Ribeiro, and close relatives appear just over the border in northern Portugal. It is frequently blended with other regional reds to add freshness and backbone.

**At the table** — its acidity makes it a fine partner for grilled fish, charcuterie and simple pork dishes.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed relatively young, when its lively fruit and acidity are at their most appealing.

name: Criolla
description:
**Criolla** is a red grape name covering a family of South American varieties descended from the vines Spanish settlers first brought to the New World. These "Criolla" grapes trace back to the old Mission-type stock and became a backbone of early winemaking across the continent.

**In the glass** — the wines are typically pale in colour, light-bodied and gently fruity, with soft tannins and modest structure. They lean toward easy, fresh, everyday drinking rather than concentration.

**Where it grows** — Argentina is the great stronghold, where Criolla varieties long dominated plantings, with related grapes found in Chile and beyond. Once destined mostly for bulk wine, they are increasingly bottled as characterful pale reds and rosés.

**At the table** — serve lightly chilled alongside empanadas, grilled sausages and casual shared plates.

**Cellaring** — made for early drinking; enjoy young while the fruit is fresh.

name: Cabernet
description:
**Cabernet** is a red grape name most often used as everyday shorthand for Cabernet Sauvignon, one of the world's most planted and celebrated black varieties. The word also broadly evokes the wider Cabernet family, which includes Cabernet Franc, the parent grape from which Cabernet Sauvignon descends.

**In the glass** — Cabernet-labelled reds typically show deep colour and blackcurrant, dark cherry and often a green or herbal note, framed by firm tannins, fresh acidity and a medium-to-full body.

**Where it grows** — grapes under this name are cultivated almost everywhere fine red wine is made, from Bordeaux and the rest of France to California, Chile, Australia, Italy and beyond, with the style shifting from restrained and structured in cooler sites to riper and fuller in warmer ones.

**At the table** — a classic match for grilled steak, lamb and hard aged cheeses.

**Cellaring** — its tannin and acidity generally allow good bottles to age and improve for years.

name: Schiava
description:
**Schiava** is a red grape from northern Italy, especially the alpine region of Alto Adige, where it is known in German as Vernatsch. It is actually a group of related varieties and has long been the traditional light red of the area.

**In the glass** — expect a pale, translucent ruby colour and delicate aromas of strawberry, cherry and sometimes a faint almond or floral note. The palate is light-bodied and gentle, with soft, low tannins and refreshing acidity.

**Where it grows** — Alto Adige and the neighbouring Trentino are its heartland, and the same grape is grown across the border in Germany's Württemberg under the name Trollinger, where it yields similarly easygoing reds.

**At the table** — versatile and food-friendly, it shines lightly chilled with cured meats, speck and lighter fare.

**Cellaring** — best drunk young and fresh, when its bright, delicate fruit is at its peak.

name: Ruchè
description:
**Ruchè** is a red grape from Piedmont in northwestern Italy, closely bound to the village of Castagnole Monferrato, where it has its own dedicated appellation. Once nearly forgotten, it has been revived as a distinctive local specialty.

**In the glass** — its hallmark is aromatic perfume: roses, violets, red berries and a warm, gently spicy note. On the palate it is medium-bodied, with moderate, silky tannins and enough acidity to keep it fresh and lifted.

**Where it grows** — it remains a small-scale rarity centred on the Monferrato hills around Castagnole in the province of Asti, with little planted elsewhere. Its scented, distinctive style sets it apart from Piedmont's more powerful reds.

**At the table** — its fragrance and soft structure suit roast poultry, pork and lighter meat dishes.

**Cellaring** — most enjoyable within a few years, while its floral aromatics are vivid, though some bottlings hold well for a while.

name: Gamba di Pernice
description:
**Gamba di Pernice** is a rare red grape from Piedmont in northwestern Italy, associated with the village of Calosso in the Asti hills. Its name, meaning "partridge leg," refers to the reddish colour of the vine's stems.

**In the glass** — it tends to give perfumed, red-fruited wines of medium body, with fresh acidity and fine, moderate tannins. Delicacy and aromatic lift are more its signature than sheer power.

**Where it grows** — it is a genuine local curiosity, cultivated in only tiny quantities around Calosso, where it has its own small appellation, and rarely seen elsewhere.

**At the table** — its fragrance and gentle structure pair nicely with poultry, pork and lighter regional dishes.

**Cellaring** — generally best enjoyed young, while its aromatic freshness is at its most expressive.

name: Frontenac Blanc
description:
**Frontenac Blanc** is a white grape developed in the United States, arising as a colour mutation within the cold-hardy Frontenac family bred in Minnesota. It was created to thrive where classic European vines struggle with harsh winters.

**In the glass** — it typically shows fresh citrus, orchard and tropical-fruit notes with lively, sometimes pronounced acidity. Wines are usually light-to-medium bodied and crisp, made in styles ranging from dry to off-dry.

**Where it grows** — it is planted mainly in the cold-climate wine regions of the northern United States and Canada, where its winter hardiness is a key advantage. It is valued by growers in areas too cold for many traditional varieties.

**At the table** — its brisk acidity suits light salads, fresh cheeses and simple seafood.

**Cellaring** — made for early drinking; enjoy it young while its fruit and acidity are fresh.

name: Frontenac Gris
description:
**Frontenac Gris** is a white grape from the United States, a colour mutation of the cold-hardy Frontenac vine developed in Minnesota. Like its siblings, it was bred to withstand very cold winters while still producing quality wine.

**In the glass** — despite the "gris" name it makes white wines, often showing peach, apricot and citrus notes with bright, vibrant acidity. It is made in styles from crisp and dry to sweeter dessert wines, and is light-to-medium in body.

**Where it grows** — it is cultivated chiefly across the cold northern United States and Canada, prized by growers in regions where winter hardiness is essential.

**At the table** — the dry versions pair well with poached fish and fresh salads, while sweeter styles complement fruit desserts.

**Cellaring** — the dry wines are best enjoyed young; sweeter, more concentrated bottlings can hold somewhat longer.

name: Torrontés
description:
**Torrontés** is a white grape best known as a signature of Argentina, particularly the high-altitude vineyards of Salta and the Cafayate valley in the north. It is really a group of related Argentine varieties, of which the most prized makes the country's most distinctive aromatic white.

**In the glass** — it is intensely perfumed, with heady aromas of rose petals, orange blossom, jasmine and stone fruit. The palate often surprises by being crisp and dry, with fresh acidity and a light-to-medium body that balances all that floral fragrance.

**Where it grows** — Argentina is its home, above all in the elevated, sun-drenched sites of Salta, where cool nights preserve its aromatics; it is also found in other Argentine regions.

**At the table** — its aromatic character makes it a lovely match for spicy Asian dishes, ceviche and fresh salads.

**Cellaring** — made to be enjoyed young, while its exuberant floral perfume is at its most vivid.

name: Malvasia del Lazio
description:
**Malvasia del Lazio** is a white grape from the region of Lazio around Rome, one of several distinct varieties that share the broad Malvasia name; it is prized locally as the more refined, aromatic partner in the traditional wines of the Roman hills.

**In the glass** — pale straw with gentle floral and stone-fruit aromatics, a suggestion of white blossom and apricot; the palate is soft and moderately full with modest acidity.

**Where it grows** — the heart of Lazio, where it is a component of Frascati and other whites of the Castelli Romani, usually blended with Trebbiano; it is notably more aromatic than the plainer Malvasia often grown alongside it.

**At the table** — pairs happily with antipasti, fried artichokes, and simple fish or poultry.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed young and fresh, ideally within a year or two of the vintage.

name: Vigiriega
description:
**Vigiriega** is a white grape of southern Spain, associated with Granada and the high vineyards of Andalusia, and closely linked to a related form grown in the Canary Islands; it is an old variety valued for holding onto freshness in a warm climate.

**In the glass** — pale in colour, with citrus and green-apple notes and a herbal, faintly saline edge; crisp and lively with bright acidity and a light body.

**Where it grows** — the province of Granada and the higher-altitude sites of Andalusia, with a version also cultivated in the Canaries; altitude tends to sharpen its mineral, fresh character.

**At the table** — grilled fish, shellfish, and light tapas.

**Cellaring** — made to be drunk young while its freshness is at its peak.

name: Malvasia Fina
description:
**Malvasia Fina** is a white grape widely planted across northern and central Portugal, especially in the Douro and Dão; despite the Malvasia name it is one of the milder, less overtly aromatic members of that broad family, valued as a dependable blending component.

**In the glass** — subtle aromas of orchard fruit, citrus and a faint nuttiness; medium-bodied with moderate acidity and a soft, rounded palate.

**Where it grows** — the Douro, where it contributes to both white Port and dry Douro whites, and the Dão, along with other parts of Portugal; it lends body and gentle fruit rather than pungent aromatics.

**At the table** — white fish, creamy poultry dishes, or served simply as an aperitif.

**Cellaring** — usually drunk young, though richer Douro examples can hold for a few years.

name: Verdicchio
description:
**Verdicchio** is a white grape from the Marche region on Italy's Adriatic coast, and one of central Italy's finest native whites; its name nods to the green tint of its berries and wines, and it anchors two celebrated appellations.

**In the glass** — pale straw with a greenish cast, offering lemon, green apple, white flowers and a signature bitter-almond note on the finish; the palate is dry and precise with lively acidity and a medium body that can gain weight through careful winemaking.

**Where it grows** — Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi, fresher and closer to the coast, and Verdicchio di Matelica, from higher inland ground and typically more structured; both lie within the Marche.

**At the table** — Adriatic fish stew, shellfish, and roast poultry.

**Cellaring** — delicious young, yet the best examples develop honeyed, nutty complexity over five to ten years.

name: Marzemino
description:
**Marzemino** is a red grape of northern Italy, most at home in Trentino, and famous enough to earn a mention in Mozart's Don Giovanni; it makes bright, approachable reds beloved in its home valleys.

**In the glass** — deep ruby, with fragrant aromas of red plum, violet and dark cherry; light to medium bodied with soft tannins and fresh acidity.

**Where it grows** — Trentino above all, with pockets in Lombardy and the Veneto; the style is generally easygoing and fruit-forward.

**At the table** — cured meats, pasta with tomato sauce, and roast pork.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed young while its vivid fruit is at its brightest.

name: Groppello
description:
**Groppello** is a red grape native to the western shore of Lake Garda in Lombardy, forming the backbone of the Valtènesi wines; it makes pale, perfumed reds and is a key ingredient in the area's delicate Chiaretto rosés.

**In the glass** — light ruby, with aromas of red berries, herbs and a hint of spice; light-bodied with gentle tannins and refreshing acidity.

**Where it grows** — the Valtènesi and Garda hills of Lombardy, both as a varietal red and blended with grapes such as Sangiovese, Barbera and Marzemino, as well as in pale Chiaretto rosé.

**At the table** — lake fish, risotto, and lighter meat dishes.

**Cellaring** — made to be drunk young and fresh.

name: Freisa
description:
**Freisa** is a red grape from Piedmont in northwest Italy and a close relative of Nebbiolo; it has a long local history and appears in many guises, from lightly sparkling and off-dry to fully dry and still.

**In the glass** — bright ruby, with aromas of raspberry, wild strawberry, rose and a savoury, faintly bitter edge; typically high in acidity and tannin with a light to medium body.

**Where it grows** — throughout Piedmont, especially around Asti, Turin and the Langhe; styles range from frothy frizzante versions to firmer, structured dry reds.

**At the table** — salumi, filled pasta such as agnolotti, and rich Piedmontese antipasti.

**Cellaring** — usually enjoyed young, though the drier, more structured versions can age gracefully for a few years.

name: Alfrocheiro
description:
**Alfrocheiro** is a red grape from central Portugal, most closely tied to the Dão, where it is valued for the deep colour and balance it brings to blends; it is sometimes known as Alfrocheiro Preto.

**In the glass** — deeply coloured, with aromas of blackberry, wild strawberry and a touch of spice; medium-bodied with smooth tannins and good acidity.

**Where it grows** — the Dão above all, along with the Alentejo and other Portuguese regions; it usually works as a blending grape, adding both colour and freshness.

**At the table** — roast lamb, grilled red meats, and hearty stews.

**Cellaring** — drinks well young, but good examples reward a few years in bottle.

name: Baga
description:
**Baga** is a red grape that defines the Bairrada region of central Portugal, thick-skinned and late-ripening; it makes deeply structured, distinctive wines and is regarded as one of the country's great characterful reds.

**In the glass** — deep in colour, with aromas of blackberry, plum, dried herbs and a savoury, earthy note; firmly tannic and high in acidity, with a medium to full body that demands time.

**Where it grows** — Bairrada above all, with scattered plantings in the Dão and elsewhere; warmer vintages and gentler winemaking help tame its natural grip.

**At the table** — the classic match is roast suckling pig, alongside other rich roast meats.

**Cellaring** — built to age, the best examples soften and grow complex over a decade or more.

name: Rufete
description:
**Rufete** is a red grape of central and northern Portugal, grown across the Beira interior and the Douro, and also known as Tinta Pinheira; it is prized for perfume and delicacy rather than sheer power.

**In the glass** — pale to medium ruby, with fragrant red-fruit and floral aromas; light-bodied with fine tannins and lively acidity.

**Where it grows** — the Beira, extending across the border into the Sierra de Salamanca in Spain, as well as the Douro; late-ripening, it does best on warm sites and adds aromatic lift to blends.

**At the table** — roast poultry, charcuterie, and lighter meat dishes.

**Cellaring** — generally best enjoyed young while its aromatics remain fresh.

name: Camarate
description:
**Camarate** is a red grape grown in Portugal, particularly in the Lisboa region to the west of the country; it is a traditional variety used mostly as part of local blends.

**In the glass** — medium ruby, with red and darker fruit aromas; moderate in body, tannin and acidity.

**Where it grows** — the Lisboa area and neighbouring parts of central-western Portugal, where it is typically blended with other native grapes rather than bottled alone.

**At the table** — grilled meats and hearty regional dishes.

**Cellaring** — usually made to be drunk young.

name: Tinta Carvalha
description:
**Tinta Carvalha** is a red grape from Portugal, most associated with the Douro valley but planted in several central and northern regions. It is very much a supporting player rather than a star, valued historically for its reliable, generous yields.

**In the glass** — it tends to give lightly coloured, soft reds with modest tannin and gentle, easygoing fruit, more useful for freshness and volume than for depth or concentration.

**Where it grows** — Portugal is its home, where it appears in field blends and everyday reds alongside more prestigious Douro varieties. It is rarely bottled on its own and seldom travels far beyond its native country.

**At the table** — pour it with simple grilled meats, sausages or a weekday stew.

**Cellaring** — this is a wine to enjoy young and fresh, while its fruit is still bright; it is not built for long keeping.

name: Procanico
description:
**Procanico** is a white grape that is the central Italian name for a strain of Trebbiano Toscano, long grown in Umbria and neighbouring areas. It matters most as a backbone of traditional Orvieto and other central Italian whites.

**In the glass** — expect a pale, fairly neutral wine with bright acidity, a light body and quiet notes of orchard fruit, white flowers and almond; charm here comes from freshness rather than aromatic drama.

**Where it grows** — Umbria is its heartland, especially around Orvieto, where it is blended with Grechetto and other local varieties. As Trebbiano it is one of Italy's most widely planted whites more broadly.

**At the table** — a natural partner for antipasti, fried vegetables, seafood and light pasta.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed young and crisp, within a year or two of the vintage.

name: Aleatico
description:
**Aleatico** is an aromatic red grape from central Italy, closely tied to the island of Elba and to Lazio, though it is also found in Puglia. Perfumed and Muscat-scented, it is prized above all for sweet, fragrant dessert reds.

**In the glass** — it is intensely floral and grapey, with rose petal, cherry and dried-fruit aromas; even dry versions carry a sweet-smelling lift, while the classic passito style is rich, silky and gently sweet with fine tannin.

**Where it grows** — Elba is its most famous home, where sun-dried grapes make the celebrated sweet red; Lazio and Puglia grow it too, sometimes in fortified or fresher styles.

**At the table** — pair the sweet versions with dark chocolate, berry tarts or ripe cheeses.

**Cellaring** — good sweet passito bottlings can age gracefully for many years, deepening in dried-fruit and spice complexity.

name: Vignoles
description:
**Vignoles** is a white French-American hybrid, also known by its breeder's code Ravat 51, that has found its real home in the vineyards of the United States. It is valued for producing aromatic, high-acid wines in cooler, harsher climates where classic European vines struggle.

**In the glass** — it is strikingly perfumed, with pineapple, apricot and honeyed tropical notes, framed by racy acidity; it works across the spectrum from crisp and off-dry to lusciously sweet.

**Where it grows** — the American Midwest, especially Missouri, along with the Finger Lakes of New York, is where it shines, often as a semi-sweet or late-harvest specialty.

**At the table** — off-dry versions flatter spicy Asian dishes, while sweet bottlings suit fruit desserts.

**Cellaring** — dry styles are best young, but the concentrated sweet, high-acid dessert wines can keep and evolve for years.

name: Catawba
description:
**Catawba** is a pink-red native American grape, dominated by Vitis labrusca, and one of the historic pillars of early American winemaking. In the nineteenth century it was among the country's most important wine grapes, celebrated for sparkling and sweet styles.

**In the glass** — it shows a distinctive "foxy," candied-grape character with high acidity and a rosy, sometimes pale colour; wines are typically off-dry to sweet, fruity and fragrant rather than serious or structured.

**Where it grows** — the eastern United States is its home, with deep roots in Ohio's Cincinnati region and later the Finger Lakes of New York, where it long fed a tradition of pink sparkling and sweet wines.

**At the table** — its sweeter styles suit brunch, fruit and light desserts, or simply a chilled glass on the porch.

**Cellaring** — this is a wine for early, cheerful drinking, not for the cellar.

name: Delaware
description:
**Delaware** is a pink-skinned American hybrid that, despite its coloured berries, is used to make white wine. A labrusca-influenced variety, it has been grown in the eastern United States since the nineteenth century and remains a familiar name in American and Japanese vineyards.

**In the glass** — it gives light, delicately fruity whites with a milder version of the grapey, "foxy" labrusca character, soft acidity and gentle floral notes, usually finished off-dry to sweet.

**Where it grows** — the eastern US is its origin, but it is especially important in Japan, where it is a leading grape for everyday white and lightly sparkling wines.

**At the table** — enjoy it as an easy aperitif or alongside light, slightly sweet dishes and fresh fruit.

**Cellaring** — drink it young while its soft fruit and freshness are at their best.

name: Humagne Rouge
description:
**Humagne Rouge** is a rustic red grape of the Swiss canton of Valais, where it is treasured as a distinctive traditional specialty. Despite the shared name it is unrelated to the white Humagne Blanche, and is in fact the same variety as the Aosta Valley's Cornalin.

**In the glass** — it is wild and savoury rather than polished, offering earthy, gamey and herbal notes over dark, slightly bitter berry fruit, with firm tannin and a robust, sometimes rugged structure.

**Where it grows** — the Valais, on the sun-warmed slopes of the upper Rhône, is its stronghold, with a small presence just across the border in Italy's Aosta Valley.

**At the table** — its gamey character calls for hearty fare like venison, cured meats and alpine dishes.

**Cellaring** — a few years in bottle can soften its rustic edges, though it is rarely a wine for very long ageing.

name: Cornalin
description:
**Cornalin** is an indigenous red grape of the Swiss Valais, also known there as Rouge du Pays, and regarded as one of the region's flagship native varieties. An old alpine grape whose exact parentage is not fully settled, it can be temperamental to grow, which keeps plantings small and prized.

**In the glass** — it produces deeply coloured, spicy reds with dark cherry and berry fruit, a peppery, savoury edge and fresh acidity, combining alpine vibrancy with real depth.

**Where it grows** — the warm, terraced slopes of the Valais along the upper Rhône are its true home, where careful growers coax reliable ripeness from difficult vintages.

**At the table** — pair it with roasted and grilled meats, game and mountain cheeses.

**Cellaring** — the best examples reward a few years of patience and can hold well in bottle, gaining spice and complexity.

name: Cabernet Blanc
description:
**Cabernet Blanc** is a white PIWI grape, a fungus-resistant crossing developed from Cabernet Sauvignon and hardy hybrid stock. Bred to withstand mildew with little or no spraying, it has become a favourite among organically and sustainably minded growers in northern Europe.

**In the glass** — it strongly recalls Sauvignon Blanc, showing gooseberry, blackcurrant leaf, green apple and grassy, tropical notes over crisp acidity and a lively, aromatic palate.

**Where it grows** — Germany is a key home, with expanding plantings across Belgium, the Netherlands, Switzerland and other cooler regions where its disease resistance is especially valuable.

**At the table** — its zesty aromatics suit goat cheese, salads, asparagus and fresh seafood.

**Cellaring** — generally made for early, refreshing drinking, though riper or barrel-aged bottlings can hold for a few years.

name: Roter Riesling
description:
**Roter Riesling** is a white grape that is an old, pink-to-red-skinned colour mutation of ordinary white Riesling. Once fairly widespread in German vineyards, it nearly vanished and is now the subject of a small but dedicated revival.

**In the glass** — it makes white wine much in the mould of classic Riesling, with bright acidity, orchard and stone fruit and floral notes, though some growers find it can offer a touch more body and gentle spice.

**Where it grows** — Germany is its home, with renewed interest in regions such as the Rheingau and Rheinhessen, where a handful of producers champion it as a historic curiosity.

**At the table** — treat it like Riesling, pairing with pork, poultry, spiced dishes and fresh fish.

**Cellaring** — like its parent it has the acidity to age, and well-made examples can develop nicely over several years.

name: Kerner
description:
**Kerner** is a white German grape, a twentieth-century crossing of the red Trollinger (Schiava) and white Riesling bred in Württemberg. Named after the poet and physician Justinus Kerner, it was created to combine Riesling-like quality with easier growing and good winter hardiness.

**In the glass** — it is aromatic and Riesling-reminiscent, with crisp acidity, notes of apple, peach and citrus and a distinctive light muscat-like floral lift, ranging from dry to off-dry.

**Where it grows** — Germany is its birthplace and remains important, but it has also found notable success in Italy's high-altitude Alto Adige and in the cool climate of Japan's Hokkaido.

**At the table** — it flatters lighter fish, poultry, salads and mildly spiced Asian dishes.

**Cellaring** — usually best enjoyed within a few years while its fresh aromatics shine, though drier, structured versions can keep longer.

name: Domina
description:
**Domina** is a red grape bred in Germany in the early twentieth century by crossing Portugieser with Pinot Noir, created to give growers deeper colour and dependable ripening in cool northern sites.

**In the glass** — it shows a dark, inky ruby, with aromas of blackberry and dark cherry over a faintly earthy edge; the palate is medium-bodied, with brisk acidity and modest, supple tannins.

**Where it grows** — it remains a German speciality, most at home in Franconia and along the Ahr, where its intense pigment is sometimes used to lend colour to lighter reds.

**At the table** — pair with roast pork, game sausages or mushroom dishes.

**Cellaring** — generally best enjoyed within a few years while the fruit is fresh, though sturdier examples hold modestly.

name: Regent
description:
**Regent** is a red grape developed in Germany as a fungus-resistant hybrid, valued by growers who want to reduce spraying, especially in organic vineyards.

**In the glass** — it is deeply coloured, with dark berry and plum fruit lifted by a touch of spice; the palate is medium-bodied, with moderate acidity and soft, rounded tannins.

**Where it grows** — mainly Germany, with further plantings across northern Europe such as England, Switzerland and Belgium, where its disease resistance suits cooler, damper climates.

**At the table** — good with grilled meats, stews and roasted vegetables.

**Cellaring** — approachable young and usually drunk within a handful of years.

name: Alicante
description:
**Alicante** is a red grape name used loosely in parts of Spain, southern France and Italy, where it has historically been applied to more than one variety — most often the widely planted Garnacha (Grenache), and sometimes the dark-fleshed teinturier Alicante Bouschet. Because it works as a regional catch-all rather than a single precise variety, wines carrying the name can differ.

**In the glass** — expect a deeply coloured red with ripe red-to-dark berry fruit, warming alcohol and gentle tannins, though the exact profile depends on which grape lies behind the label.

**Where it grows** — the name turns up around the western Mediterranean, in Spain and neighbouring regions of southern Europe.

**At the table** — hearty stews and grilled meats.

**Cellaring** — usually made for early, generous drinking.

name: Niagara
description:
**Niagara** is a white grape from the United States, a member of the native labrusca-derived hybrids that counts Concord among its parents and is planted widely across the eastern states.

**In the glass** — it is pale gold, with the pronounced "foxy," candied-grape aroma typical of labrusca varieties; the palate is soft and low in acidity, and it is frequently finished with some sweetness.

**Where it grows** — the northeastern US and Ontario, particularly around the Great Lakes, with much of the crop going to grape juice as well as wine.

**At the table** — try it with spicy dishes or simply chilled with fresh fruit.

**Cellaring** — made to be drunk young and fresh.

name: Cayuga White
description:
**Cayuga White** is a white grape bred in the United States at Cornell University's research station in New York, one of a family of cold-hardy hybrids created for the region's demanding climate.

**In the glass** — it is light and aromatic, with apple, melon and floral notes; the palate is crisp and light-bodied, and it is often made in an off-dry style.

**Where it grows** — chiefly the northeastern US, especially the Finger Lakes of New York, where its disease resistance and cold tolerance are prized.

**At the table** — pairs happily with lighter poultry, salads or spicy Asian fare.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed young while its aromatics are lively.

name: Teroldego
description:
**Teroldego** is a red grape native to the Trentino region of northern Italy, long associated with the gravelly Campo Rotaliano plain where it makes the area's signature red.

**In the glass** — it is deeply coloured, with dark berry, black cherry and a note of pine or tar; the palate is medium to full-bodied, with fresh acidity and fine, slightly grippy tannins.

**Where it grows** — its heartland is Trentino, though plantings have spread to other Italian regions and to a few New World growers.

**At the table** — braised beef, cured meats and hard cheeses.

**Cellaring** — enjoyable young, but the better bottlings gain complexity over several years.

name: Avesso
description:
**Avesso** is a white grape from northern Portugal, one of the varieties used in the Vinho Verde region, particularly its warmer, more inland pockets.

**In the glass** — it is pale straw, with stone-fruit and citrus aromas; compared with many Vinho Verde whites it is fuller and rounder, keeping bright acidity alongside a little more body.

**Where it grows** — mainly the Vinho Verde region of Portugal.

**At the table** — a natural with grilled fish and seafood.

**Cellaring** — best drunk young and fresh, though its fuller frame gives slightly more staying power than the lightest Vinho Verde grapes.

name: Vernaccia di San Gimignano
description:
**Vernaccia di San Gimignano** is a white grape from Tuscany, famous as the variety behind the wine of the same name — one of the first Italian wines to earn DOC recognition, back in 1966.

**In the glass** — it is pale gold, with citrus, green apple and a characteristic almond note; the palate is dry, crisp and medium-bodied, often closing with a gentle bitter-almond twist.

**Where it grows** — closely tied to the hills around the town of San Gimignano in central Tuscany.

**At the table** — seafood, poultry and Tuscan antipasti.

**Cellaring** — usually enjoyed young, though the more structured examples can develop over a few years.

name: Trebbiano di Soave
description:
**Trebbiano di Soave** is a white grape of the Veneto in northern Italy, one of the traditional components of Soave; genetically it is the same variety as the Verdicchio grown further south.

**In the glass** — it is pale, with subtle white-flower, citrus and almond aromas; the palate is dry, medium-bodied and fresh, with restrained but appealing character.

**Where it grows** — the Veneto, in Soave and around Lake Garda, where a related name, Turbiana, is used for the wines of Lugana.

**At the table** — risotto, freshwater fish and light pasta dishes.

**Cellaring** — mostly enjoyed young, though good examples can age gracefully.

name: St. Laurent
description:
**St. Laurent** is a red grape most associated with Austria, a member of the Pinot family and a parent of the widely grown Zweigelt.

**In the glass** — it shows a moderately deep ruby, with dark cherry and berry fruit and an earthy, Pinot-like perfume; the palate is medium-bodied, with fresh acidity and soft, silky tannins.

**Where it grows** — chiefly Austria, notably the Thermenregion and Burgenland, plus the Czech Republic, Germany and other parts of central Europe.

**At the table** — roast duck, pork and mushroom dishes.

**Cellaring** — lovely young, but serious versions reward a few years in the cellar.

name: Picpoul Blanc
description:
**Picpoul Blanc** is a white grape of southern France, best known as the grape behind Picpoul de Pinet in the Languedoc; its name is often read as "lip-stinger," a nod to its zesty acidity.

**In the glass** — it is pale with a greenish tint, offering citrus, green apple and a saline, floral lift; the palate is light-bodied, dry and refreshingly high in acidity.

**Where it grows** — chiefly the Languedoc coast near the Mediterranean, with scattered plantings elsewhere in southern France.

**At the table** — a classic match for oysters and other shellfish.

**Cellaring** — made for young, fresh drinking.

name: Marselan
description:
**Marselan** is a red grape bred in the south of France in 1961 by crossing Cabernet Sauvignon with Grenache, named after the coastal town of Marseillan. The idea was to marry Cabernet's structure with Grenache's warmth and generosity, and it took decades for growers to appreciate the result.

**In the glass** — deep, saturated purple with aromas of blackberry, black cherry and a touch of herbs; the palate is full and smooth, with ripe tannins and enough freshness to stay lively.

**Where it grows** — its home is the Languedoc-Roussillon, but its most striking success story is China, where it has become something of a signature red; you'll also find scattered plantings in California, Argentina and Brazil.

**At the table** — lovely with grilled lamb, beef or anything off the barbecue.

**Cellaring** — approachable young but happy to rest for several years, softening into a rounder, more savoury wine.

name: Perricone
description:
**Perricone** is a red grape native to Sicily, also known there as Pignatello, long valued as a workhorse for blending and for adding backbone to fortified Marsala.

**In the glass** — dark-hued and rustic, offering red and black berry fruit alongside earthy, herbal notes; it tends toward firm tannins and moderate acidity, giving a sturdy, savoury feel.

**Where it grows** — almost entirely in western Sicily, where it plays a supporting role to Nero d'Avola and appears in traditional Marsala, though a handful of producers now bottle it on its own.

**At the table** — pairs well with braised meats, aged cheese and hearty tomato-based pasta.

**Cellaring** — its tannin lets it hold and improve over a few years, but most versions are enjoyable within their first several years.

name: Arrufiac
description:
**Arrufiac** is a white grape from South West France, closely tied to the Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh and Saint-Mont appellations, where it is grown almost exclusively as a blending partner.

**In the glass** — pale and fresh, with citrus and delicate floral notes; its main gift is crisp, zippy acidity that lifts and tightens a blend.

**Where it grows** — very much a local speciality of Gascony and the foothills near the Pyrenees, where it is folded together with Gros Manseng and Petit Courbu rather than bottled alone.

**At the table** — a natural match for oysters, shellfish and simply grilled fish.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed young, while its bright, nervy freshness is at its peak.

name: Courbu
description:
**Courbu** is a white grape of South West France, found in the patchwork of appellations around Béarn and the Pyrenean foothills, where it has long been a blending companion to the Manseng grapes.

**In the glass** — aromatic and gently floral, with citrus, orchard fruit and a hint of honey; it carries good acidity and a certain roundness that fleshes out a blend.

**Where it grows** — mainly in Jurançon, Pacherenc du Vic-Bilh, Saint-Mont and Béarn, where growers prize it for the perfume and texture it adds to both dry and sweet wines.

**At the table** — try it with river fish, poultry or soft creamy cheeses.

**Cellaring** — usually best drunk young, though richer sweet examples can hold for a good while.

name: Codega do Larinho
description:
**Codega do Larinho** is a white grape from Portugal's Douro Valley, one of the region's traditional varieties used in both white Port and dry white Douro blends.

**In the glass** — it leans toward soft stone fruit and gentle citrus, with a rounded, easygoing body and relatively low acidity that gives generosity rather than tension.

**Where it grows** — almost entirely in the terraced schist vineyards of the Douro, where it is typically co-planted and blended with other regional whites to build breadth and aroma.

**At the table** — good alongside grilled fish, chicken or lightly spiced dishes.

**Cellaring** — generally at its best young and fresh, while its fruit is bright.

name: Teran
description:
**Teran** is a red grape of the Istrian peninsula, shared across Croatia and Slovenia, and part of the wider Refosco family known for deeply coloured, high-acid reds grown on the region's iron-rich red soils.

**In the glass** — inky and vivid, with sour cherry, wild berry and a distinctly earthy, mineral streak; the hallmark is racy, mouth-watering acidity backed by firm tannin.

**Where it grows** — the terra rossa vineyards of Istria are its heartland, where it is regarded as a proud local speciality on both sides of the border.

**At the table** — made for the region's cured ham and grilled or braised meats.

**Cellaring** — bright and juicy young, though its acidity and structure allow the better bottlings to hold for several years.

name: Manseng Noir
description:
**Manseng Noir** is a rare red grape from South West France, a near-forgotten variety that a few growers have worked to bring back from the edge of extinction.

**In the glass** — it tends to give a light- to medium-bodied red with fresh red fruit, a peppery lift and lively acidity rather than heavy weight.

**Where it grows** — confined to scattered plantings in its South West French homeland, where it remains very much a curiosity for growers interested in reviving old local varieties.

**At the table** — suits lighter meats, charcuterie and simple bistro fare.

**Cellaring** — best enjoyed young, for its freshness and easy charm.

name: Neuburger
description:
**Neuburger** is a white grape of Austria, a natural crossing of Roter Veltliner and Silvaner that has become a modest but characterful part of the country's vineyards.

**In the glass** — recognisable for its nutty character, with orchard fruit and soft floral notes; it is typically medium-bodied with gentle, unaggressive acidity, giving a mellow, rounded feel.

**Where it grows** — most at home in Austria's Wachau, Thermenregion and Weinviertel, where it makes everything from dry table wines to riper, fuller styles.

**At the table** — pleasant with roast chicken, pork or creamy vegetable dishes.

**Cellaring** — generally best in its first few years, while its nutty freshness shows well, though richer examples can hold a little longer.

name: Garanoir
description:
**Garanoir** is a red grape created in Switzerland, a crossing of Gamay and Reichensteiner bred at the Changins research station and a sibling of the better-known Gamaret.

**In the glass** — deeply coloured with juicy dark-berry fruit, a supple, rounded texture and notably soft, low tannin, making for an approachable, fruit-forward red.

**Where it grows** — grown chiefly in French-speaking Switzerland, where it is often blended with Gamaret or Pinot Noir to add colour and easy drinkability.

**At the table** — a friendly partner for charcuterie, roast meats and cheese.

**Cellaring** — designed for early, easy drinking rather than long ageing.

name: Altesse
description:
**Altesse** is a white grape of the French Alps, best known as the noble variety of Savoie, where it is also called Roussette and gives the region's most serious whites.

**In the glass** — expressive and fine, with citrus, pear, a touch of honey and a nutty, almost herbal edge; the palate is bright and mineral, with fresh acidity and a satisfying weight.

**Where it grows** — the vineyards of Savoie are its home, where it stars in Roussette de Savoie and Seyssel, capturing the crisp, alpine mountain character growers prize.

**At the table** — excellent with lake fish, alpine cheeses and creamy gratins.

**Cellaring** — enjoyable young but unusually age-worthy for a white, gaining honeyed, nutty depth with a few years in the cellar.

name: Lacrima
description:
**Lacrima** is a red grape of Italy's Marche region, celebrated in the small Lacrima di Morro d'Alba appellation for producing one of the most floral and aromatic reds in the country.

**In the glass** — instantly recognisable for its intense scent of roses and violets, followed by juicy purple and blue fruit; the palate is soft and gentle, with supple tannins and a perfumed, almost sweet-fruited charm.

**Where it grows** — a genuine local speciality around the town of Morro d'Alba in the Marche, where it is grown almost nowhere else.

**At the table** — lovely with cured meats, medium-rich pasta and mild cheeses.

**Cellaring** — very much a wine to drink young, while its extraordinary floral aromatics are fresh and vivid.

name: Baco Blanc
description:
**Baco Blanc** is a white grape bred in France as a hybrid, created to combine the aromatics of European vines with the disease resistance of American ones. It matters chiefly as a workhorse of Armagnac, the brandy region of Gascony, where it was long the mainstay distilling grape.

**In the glass** — as a still wine it is fairly neutral and tart, with modest floral and green-fruit notes; its real virtue is high acidity and clean, low-alcohol juice that distils well.

**Where it grows** — its home is southwest France, above all the Armagnac appellations, where growers value its reliability and resistance in a damp climate. It is rarely seen far beyond there, and almost never as a varietal table wine.

**At the table** — the eaux-de-vie it yields suit foie gras, prunes and dark chocolate rather than the dinner plate.

**Cellaring** — the base wine is made to be distilled young, but the Armagnac it becomes can age for decades in cask and bottle.

name: Folle Blanche
description:
**Folle Blanche** is a white grape from France, historically important in both the Loire and Gascony as a base for brandy. It once underpinned much of Cognac and Armagnac before phylloxera pushed growers toward hardier alternatives.

**In the glass** — it gives pale, lean wine with racing acidity, restrained citrus and green-apple fruit and a distinctly bracing, almost austere character.

**Where it grows** — around Nantes at the mouth of the Loire it makes the crisp, tart white Gros Plant du Pays Nantais, a classic partner to the local shellfish; in Gascony it still feeds Armagnac stills. It appears only sparingly elsewhere.

**At the table** — its sharp freshness is tailor-made for oysters, mussels and other briny seafood.

**Cellaring** — best drunk young and cold, while its zippy acidity is at its liveliest.

name: Nero Buono
description:
**Nero Buono** is a red grape native to the Lazio region of central Italy, associated in particular with the area around Cori, south of Rome. It is a local speciality rarely encountered outside its home ground.

**In the glass** — it typically gives a deeply coloured red with dark-berry fruit, gentle spice and a fairly full, sturdy structure.

**Where it grows** — it is grown almost entirely in Lazio, where a handful of producers champion it both on its own and in blends. Plantings are small and it remains something of a regional rarity.

**At the table** — a natural match for hearty pasta dishes, roasts and aged cheeses.

**Cellaring** — most examples are made to be enjoyed within a few years, though sturdier bottlings can hold for a while longer.

name: Schioppettino
description:
**Schioppettino** is a red grape from Friuli in northeastern Italy, near the Slovenian border. Once nearly lost, it was rescued by a small group of dedicated growers and has become a proud symbol of the region's revival of native varieties.

**In the glass** — it is prized for its peppery, spicy aroma alongside dark cherry and red berry, with fresh acidity, fine-grained tannin and a lively, medium-bodied frame.

**Where it grows** — its heartland is eastern Friuli, especially around the villages where it was replanted; it is only occasionally found beyond that corner of Italy.

**At the table** — its spice and freshness suit grilled meats, game and rich, savoury stews.

**Cellaring** — approachable young, the better bottlings gain complexity with several years in the cellar.

name: Catarratto
description:
**Catarratto** is a white grape from Sicily, where it is one of the island's most widely planted varieties. Long a backbone of Marsala and everyday blends, it has increasingly been taken seriously as a characterful dry white in its own right.

**In the glass** — expect a medium-bodied white with citrus, orchard fruit and a subtle herbal or savoury edge, carried by fresh acidity and often a faint saline note.

**Where it grows** — it is grown almost entirely on Sicily, thriving in the warm, sunny west of the island; styles range from simple, crisp bottlings to more ambitious, textured wines.

**At the table** — a fine partner for grilled fish, seafood pasta and Mediterranean vegetable dishes.

**Cellaring** — generally best enjoyed young and fresh, though skin-contact and more serious examples can develop with a little age.

name: Petite Arvine
description:
**Petite Arvine** is a white grape closely tied to the Valais in the Swiss Alps, where it is one of the country's most treasured native varieties. It ranks among the most distinctive and age-worthy of Switzerland's white grapes.

**In the glass** — it is known for aromas of apricot, citrus and white flowers, a vibrant acidity, and a signature salty, savoury finish that gives it real presence.

**Where it grows** — its heartland is the sun-drenched Rhône valley slopes of the Valais, where it is made both bone-dry and as sweet late-harvest wine; a little is also grown just across the border in Italy's Aosta Valley.

**At the table** — dry versions pair beautifully with alpine cheeses, freshwater fish and creamy dishes.

**Cellaring** — the finest dry and sweet examples reward several years of patience.

name: Picolit
description:
**Picolit** is a white grape from Friuli in northeastern Italy, famous for producing a rare and highly prized sweet dessert wine. Its renown far outstrips its tiny production, partly because the vine naturally sets very few berries, making it scarce and costly.

**In the glass** — as a sweet wine it offers delicate aromas of honey, apricot, dried flowers and candied peel, with a graceful sweetness kept in balance by gentle acidity and a refined, elegant texture rather than sheer richness.

**Where it grows** — it is grown almost exclusively in Friuli, especially the Colli Orientali hills, where the grapes are often left to concentrate before pressing. It is seldom found elsewhere.

**At the table** — lovely with pastries, almond desserts, or simply on its own as a meditation wine.

**Cellaring** — good examples age gracefully for many years, deepening in colour and complexity.
